scenes.text: A city metro raises fares from ₹10 to ₹12. Ridership falls from 100,000 to 80,000 a day.
Did revenue rise or fall? Elasticity tells us before the money is counted.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Law of demand**: other things equal, quantity demanded falls as price rises (exceptions: Giffen goods, Veblen goods)
- **Price elasticity** Ed = %ΔQ/%ΔP (negative; we often quote |Ed|)
- **Arc (midpoint) elasticity** = (ΔQ/average Q)/(ΔP/average P)
- **Point elasticity** = (dQ/dP)(P/Q)
- |Ed| > 1 elastic: price rise lowers total revenue; |Ed| < 1 inelastic: price rise raises revenue; |Ed| = 1: revenue unchanged
- **Income elasticity**: > 0 normal (> 1 luxury), < 0 inferior. **Cross elasticity**: > 0 substitutes, < 0 complements

steps.title: Solved: the metro
steps.body:
P: 10 → 12; Q: 100 → 80 (thousand).

- Arc: ΔQ/avgQ = −20/90 = −0.222; ΔP/avgP = 2/11 = 0.182 ⇒ **Ed ≈ −1.22** (elastic)
- Revenue: 10 × 100 = 1,000 → 12 × 80 = 960 ⇒ **falls** ✓ consistent with elastic demand

steps.title: Solved: linear demand
steps.body:
Q = 100 − 2P.

- At P = 20: Q = 60; Ed = −2 × 20/60 = **−0.67** (inelastic)
- Unit elastic where P/Q = 1/2 ⇒ P = 25, Q = 50 (the midpoint)
- Above P = 25 demand is elastic; below, inelastic

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating slope as elasticity (a straight line has constant slope but changing elasticity).
- Using different bases for % changes in arc calculations.
- Calling a good with income elasticity 0.5 a luxury.
- Forgetting 'other things equal' when explaining shifts vs movements.

bands.text: Perfectly inelastic: price changes don't change quantity (e.g. life-saving drugs, short run).
Inelastic: a price rise RAISES total revenue.
Unit elastic: revenue unchanged by small price changes.
Elastic: a price rise LOWERS total revenue (many close substitutes).

quiz.why: If |Ed| < 1, demand is inelastic: quantity falls proportionally less than the price rises. So total revenue rises.

quiz.q: Income elasticity of an inferior good is:
quiz.why: An inferior good has negative income elasticity: demand falls as income rises.

quiz.q: Cross elasticity of tea and coffee is likely:
quiz.why: Tea and coffee are substitutes. If the price of one rises, demand for the other rises, so cross elasticity is positive.

quiz.q: On a straight-line demand curve, elasticity at the midpoint is:
quiz.why: On a straight-line demand curve, elasticity is 1 (unit) at the midpoint. It is above 1 above the midpoint and below 1 below it.
|Ed| = %ΔQ ÷ %ΔP = 10 ÷ 5 = 2, so demand is elastic.

scenes.text: Ira has ₹100 left for snacks: samosas or ice cream.
She's happiest when the last rupee spent on each gives equal extra satisfaction.

steps.title: Cardinal utility
steps.body:
- Total utility (TU) and marginal utility (MU = ΔTU/ΔQ)
- **Law of diminishing marginal utility**: MU falls as more units are consumed
- One good: buy until **MU = P** (in money terms)
- Two goods: **equi-marginal principle** — MUx/Px = MUy/Py, with income fully spent
- Demand curve slopes down because MU diminishes

steps.title: Solved: equi-marginal
steps.body:
Px = ₹10, Py = ₹20. MUx for units 1–4: 50, 40, 30, 20. MUy: 100, 80, 60, 40. Income ₹70.

- MU per rupee: x: 5, 4, 3, 2; y: 5, 4, 3, 2
- Choose highest ratios first until ₹70 is spent: x1 (5), y1 (5), x2 (4), y2 (4) costs 10 + 20 + 10 + 20 = 60; next ratio 3: x3 costs 10 ⇒ total ₹70
- Equilibrium **x = 3, y = 2**: MUx/Px = 3 = MUy/Py = 60/20 = 3 ✓

steps.title: Solved: water–diamond paradox
steps.body: Water has huge total utility but low marginal utility (it is plentiful); diamonds have low total utility but high marginal utility (scarce). **Price reflects marginal, not total, utility.**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating MU across goods without dividing by price.
- Confusing total and marginal utility.
- Forgetting the budget must be exhausted.
- Assuming utility is literally measurable (cardinal approach is a simplification; ordinal approach avoids it).

statements.s: Diminishing marginal utility means total utility falls.
statements.why: TU rises at a decreasing rate until MU becomes zero.

statements.s: Price depends on marginal utility, not total utility.
When MU = 0, total utility is at its maximum.

quiz.why: Marginal utility is the extra utility from one more unit: ΔTU/ΔQ.

quiz.q: TU is maximum when MU is:
quiz.why: Total utility is at its maximum when marginal utility is zero. After that MU is negative and TU falls.

quiz.q: Equi-marginal condition with prices ₹5 and ₹10 and MUx = 20 requires MUy =
quiz.why: The equi-marginal rule says MUx/Px = MUy/Py. With 20/5 = 4, MUy/10 must be 4, so MUy = 40.
The water–diamond paradox is explained by marginal utility. Water is abundant, so its marginal utility is low, while diamonds are scarce, so theirs is high.
Cardinal utility assumes that utility can be measured in numbers (utils). Ordinal utility only ranks preferences.

lessons.title: Indifference curves and the budget line

scenes.text: A student with ₹1,000 a month chooses between books (₹200) and movie tickets (₹100).
Her best bundle is where her highest indifference curve just touches her budget line.

steps.title: Ordinal approach
steps.body:
- **Indifference curve (IC)**: bundles giving equal satisfaction; downward sloping, convex (diminishing MRS), never intersect; higher ICs preferred
- **MRSxy** = −dy/dx along an IC = MUx/MUy
- **Budget line**: Px·x + Py·y = M; slope −Px/Py
- **Equilibrium** (tangency): MRSxy = Px/Py, on the budget line
- Perfect substitutes → straight-line ICs; perfect complements → L-shaped ICs

steps.title: Solved: Cobb–Douglas choice
steps.body:
U = xy, M = 100, Px = 2, Py = 5.

- MRS = MUx/MUy = y/x; set y/x = 2/5 ⇒ y = 0.4x
- Budget: 2x + 5(0.4x) = 100 ⇒ 4x = 100 ⇒ **x = 25, y = 10**
- Shortcut for U = x^a y^(1−a): x = aM/Px, y = (1 − a)M/Py

steps.title: Solved: budget line changes
steps.body:
- Income doubles → parallel outward shift
- Px falls → line pivots outward on the x-axis (y-intercept unchanged)
- Both prices and income double → **no change** in the budget line (real income constant)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing intersecting indifference curves (violates transitivity).
- Writing MRS = Py/Px.
- Forgetting that a corner solution can occur with perfect substitutes.
- Confusing a price change (pivot) with an income change (shift).

activity.prompt: U = x^0.5 y^0.5, income ₹200, Px = ₹4, Py = ₹10. How many units of x are chosen?

quiz.why: At consumer equilibrium, the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line: MRS = Px/Py.
Indifference curves are convex because of the diminishing MRS. The consumer is willing to give up less of y for each extra x.

quiz.q: Perfect complements have ICs that are:
quiz.why: Perfect complements are consumed in fixed proportions, such as left and right shoes, so their indifference curves are L-shaped.

quiz.q: If income rises with prices fixed, the budget line:
quiz.why: If income rises with prices fixed, the budget line shifts outward in parallel. Its slope depends only on the price ratio.
The slope of the budget line is −Px/Py, the price ratio, when x is on the horizontal axis.

lessons.title: Income and substitution effects; consumer surplus

scenes.text: When onion prices triple, families buy fewer onions — partly because onions are now relatively costly, partly because they feel poorer.
Economists separate these two forces: substitution and income effects.

steps.title: Decomposition
steps.body:
Price effect = **substitution effect** + **income effect**.

- Substitution effect (holding real income constant — Hicks: same utility; Slutsky: same purchasing power) is **always negative**: a price rise reduces quantity
- Income effect: negative for normal goods (reinforces), positive for inferior goods (opposes)
- **Giffen good**: inferior good whose positive income effect outweighs the substitution effect ⇒ upward-sloping demand
- **Slutsky equation** (compact form): ∂x/∂Px = ∂x/∂Px|compensated − x·∂x/∂M

steps.title: Solved: Slutsky compensation
steps.body:
A consumer buys 10 units of x at Px = ₹5. Price rises to ₹6.

- Slutsky compensation = Δ P × original x = 1 × 10 = **₹10** — the extra income that lets her just afford the old bundle
- With that extra ₹10 she might buy 9 units (substitution effect −1); without it she buys 8 (income effect −1). Total effect −2.

steps.title: Solved: consumer surplus
steps.body:
Demand P = 50 − Q; market price ₹20.

- Q = 30
- CS = ½ × 30 × (50 − 20) = **₹450**
- If price falls to ₹10, Q = 40 and CS = ½ × 40 × 40 = ₹800

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the substitution effect can be positive.
- Calling every inferior good a Giffen good.
- Computing CS using price instead of (maximum willingness − price).
- Mixing up Hicks and Slutsky compensation.

activity.prompt: For a price RISE, classify the income effect.

items.text: Inferior good (coarse grain for poor households)

quiz.q: The substitution effect of a price rise on quantity is:
quiz.why: The substitution effect of a price rise is always negative: relatively dearer goods are bought less, and income is held fixed in utility terms.

options: inferior with a strong income effect
quiz.why: A Giffen good is an inferior good whose income effect is strong enough to outweigh the substitution effect. So demand rises when the price rises.
Consumer surplus is the area below the demand curve and above the price. It is what consumers would be willing to pay minus what they pay.

quiz.q: Slutsky compensation for a ₹2 price rise on 15 units:
quiz.why: Slutsky compensation is ΔP × quantity bought = ₹2 × 15 = ₹30. It lets the consumer afford the original bundle.

quiz.q: For a normal good, the income effect of a price fall:
quiz.why: For a normal good, a price fall raises real income, so the income effect increases the quantity demanded. The consumer feels richer and buys more.

questions.q: The law of demand states price and quantity demanded are:
questions.why: The law of demand says price and quantity demanded are inversely related, other things being equal.

questions.q: A good with income elasticity 1.8 is a:
questions.why: Income elasticity above 1, such as 1.8, means demand rises more than proportionally with income. That is a luxury good.

questions.q: Indifference curves never:
questions.why: Indifference curves never intersect, because of transitivity. Intersecting curves would give contradictory rankings.

questions.q: Price falls from ₹20 to ₹18; quantity rises 100 to 110 (point method on initial values). |Ed|:
questions.why: Price falls 2/20 = 10% and quantity rises 10/100 = 10%. |Ed| = 10% ÷ 10% = 1.

questions.q: MRS = 3 and Px/Py = 2. The consumer should buy:
questions.why: MRS = 3 is greater than Px/Py = 2. The consumer values x more than its relative price, so buy more x and less y.

questions.q: Cross elasticity of cars and petrol is:
questions.why: Cars and petrol are complements, so a price rise in one lowers demand for the other. Cross elasticity is negative.

questions.q: Assertion: Total revenue is maximum where demand is unit elastic. Reason: Marginal revenue is zero at unit elasticity.
questions.why: MR = P(1 − 1/|Ed|), which is zero at unit elasticity. Total revenue is maximum where MR = 0, so both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: U = x^0.3 y^0.7, M = ₹1,000, Py = ₹10. Quantity of y:
questions.why: For a Cobb–Douglas utility, the consumer spends the share 0.7 of income on y. So y = 0.7 × 1000 ÷ 10 = 70.

questions.q: Demand Q = 200 − 4P. Price at which |Ed| = 1:
questions.why: |Ed| = 4P/Q = 1 gives 4P = 200 − 4P, so P = 25. That is the midpoint of the linear demand curve.

questions.q: Case: Salt's price doubles; quantity hardly changes. Total spending on salt:
questions.why: If quantity hardly changes when the price doubles, demand is near perfectly inelastic. So total spending on salt roughly doubles.

questions.q: P = 80 − 2Q; price ₹40. Consumer surplus:
questions.why: At P = 40, 40 = 80 − 2Q gives Q = 20. Consumer surplus = ½ × 20 × (80 − 40) = ₹400.

questions.q: Arc elasticity: P 4 → 6, Q 120 → 80:
questions.why: With midpoints, %ΔQ = −40/100 = −0.4 and %ΔP = 2/5 = 0.4. So arc elasticity = −0.4/0.4 = −1.

questions.q: With perfect substitutes U = x + y, Px = 3, Py = 4, M = 120, optimal bundle:
questions.why: With perfect substitutes, buy the good with the lower price per util. Px = 3 < Py = 4, so spend it all on x: 120 ÷ 3 = 40 units of x and 0 of y.

questions.q: For a Giffen good, a price fall leads to:
questions.why: For a Giffen good, a price fall lowers the quantity demanded, because the strong income effect outweighs the substitution effect. Its demand slopes upward.

lessons.title: Production: short run and returns to scale

scenes.text: A small dhaba adds a second, third and fourth cook to the same kitchen.
Output rises — but each extra cook adds less than the one before. Diminishing returns.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- Short run: at least one fixed input. Total, average and marginal product (TP, AP, MP)
- **Law of variable proportions**: MP eventually diminishes. Stage I (AP rising), Stage II (AP falling, MP ≥ 0 — rational stage), Stage III (MP < 0)
- MP cuts AP at AP's maximum
- Long run: all inputs variable; **isoquants** and MRTS = MPL/MPK
- **Returns to scale** for Q = A L^α K^β: α + β > 1 increasing, = 1 constant, < 1 decreasing

steps.title: Solved: MP and AP
steps.body:
TP for L = 1…5: 10, 24, 36, 44, 48.

- MP: 10, 14, 12, 8, 4
- AP: 10, 12, 12, 11, 9.6
- MP peaks at L = 2; AP is maximal at L = 2–3 where MP ≈ AP

steps.title: Solved: returns to scale
steps.body:
- Q = 5 L^0.6 K^0.4: α + β = 1 ⇒ **constant**
- Q = L^0.7 K^0.5: 1.2 ⇒ **increasing** (doubling inputs multiplies output by 2^1.2 ≈ 2.3)
- Q = L^0.3 K^0.3: 0.6 ⇒ **decreasing**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing diminishing returns (short run, one input) with decreasing returns to scale (long run, all inputs).
- Thinking a firm operates in Stage I or III.
- Saying AP falls when MP falls (only when MP < AP).

activity.prompt: Match each production function to its returns to scale.

quiz.why: MP cuts AP at AP's maximum. This is the marginal–average rule: when MP is above AP, AP rises, and when below, AP falls.
A rational producer operates in Stage II, where MP is still positive but AP is falling. In Stage I it is better to add more of the variable input, and in Stage III MP is negative.
The exponents add to 0.4 + 0.6 = 1, so the production function shows constant returns to scale.

quiz.q: Law of variable proportions is a ___ concept:
quiz.why: The law of variable proportions is a short-run concept, as at least one input is fixed while another varies.
MRTS (marginal rate of technical substitution) = MPL/MPK, the slope of the isoquant.

scenes.text: A print shop pays ₹100 a day rent whether it prints 1 page or 1,000.
As volume grows, rent per page falls — but overtime and machine strain eventually push costs back up: the U-shaped AC curve.

steps.title: Relationships
steps.body:
- TC = TFC + TVC; AC = AFC + AVC; MC = dTC/dQ
- AFC falls continuously; AVC and AC are U-shaped (diminishing returns)
- **MC cuts AVC and AC at their minimum points**
- Long-run AC is the envelope of short-run AC curves; U-shape from economies then diseconomies of scale

steps.title: Solved: from TC to curves
steps.body:
TC = 100 + 10Q + Q².

- MC = 10 + 2Q; AVC = 10 + Q; AC = 100/Q + 10 + Q
- Min AC: dAC/dQ = −100/Q² + 1 = 0 ⇒ Q = 10, AC = 30 (and MC = 30 ✓)
- Min AVC at Q → 0, value ₹10 (shutdown price)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Letting MC cut AC at AC's maximum.
- Including fixed cost in MC.
- Thinking AFC eventually rises.
- Confusing diseconomies of scale (long run) with diminishing returns (short run).

activity.prompt: TC = 200 + 5Q + 2Q². At what output is average cost minimised?

quiz.why: MC cuts AC at AC's minimum. When MC is below AC, AC falls, and when above, AC rises.
AFC = TFC ÷ Q falls continuously as output rises, because the fixed cost is spread over more units.
MC is the derivative of TC. With TC = 50 + 4Q, MC = 4.

quiz.q: LRAC is the ___ of SRAC curves:
quiz.why: The long-run average cost curve (LRAC) is the envelope of the short-run average cost curves. It is also called the planning curve.

quiz.q: If MC < AC, then AC is:
quiz.why: If MC is below AC, the marginal unit pulls the average down, so AC is falling.

story.title: Tomato farmers vs the only metro

scenes.text: Thousands of tomato farmers each take the mandi price as given.
A city's only metro operator sets its own fare. Different structures, different outcomes.

steps.title: Perfect competition
steps.body:
- Many firms, homogeneous product, free entry, price takers: P = AR = MR
- Profit max: **P = MC** with MC rising
- Short run: shut down if P < min AVC
- Long run: entry/exit drives P to **min AC** — normal profit, productive and allocative efficiency

steps.title: Monopoly
steps.body:
- Single seller, barriers to entry; downward-sloping demand ⇒ MR < P
- Profit max: **MR = MC**; price from the demand curve
- **Lerner index** = (P − MC)/P = 1/|Ed| ⇒ monopolist always produces on the elastic part of demand
- **Deadweight loss**: output below the competitive level
- **Price discrimination**: first degree (perfect), second (by quantity), third (by market segment; higher price where demand is less elastic)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Setting P = MC for a monopolist.
- Reading monopoly price off the MR curve.
- Shutting down when P < AC (rather than P < AVC) in the short run.
- Thinking monopolists charge the highest possible price.

activity.prompt: A monopolist faces P = 120 − Q and MC = ₹40. What price does it charge (₹)?

quiz.why: In perfect competition the firm is a price taker, so P = MR. Profit is maximised where MR = MC, which gives P = MC.
In the short run, a firm shuts down if price is below the minimum AVC, since it can't cover its variable cost.

quiz.q: Monopoly MR for linear demand has:
options: the same intercept and twice the slope
quiz.why: For linear demand P = a − bQ, MR = a − 2bQ. It has the same intercept and twice the slope.
The Lerner index (P − MC)/P equals 1/|Ed| at the monopolist's optimum. It measures market power.

quiz.q: Third-degree discrimination charges more in the market with:
quiz.why: In third-degree price discrimination, charge the higher price in the market with less elastic demand. The price depends inversely on elasticity.

scenes.text: Two big telecom firms watch each other's tariffs closely.
Each firm's best move depends on the other's — strategic interaction studied by game theory.

steps.title: Models
steps.body:
- **Cournot**: firms choose quantities simultaneously. With P = a − bQ and common MC = c, each firm produces (a − c)/(3b); total 2(a − c)/(3b) — between monopoly and competition
- **Bertrand**: price competition with identical products ⇒ P = MC
- **Kinked demand** (Sweezy): rivals match price cuts but not rises ⇒ gap in MR ⇒ price rigidity
- **Game theory**: dominant strategy; **Nash equilibrium** (no player gains by deviating alone); **prisoner's dilemma** — individually rational choices give a collectively worse outcome; cartels are unstable

steps.title: Solved: Cournot duopoly
steps.body:
P = 120 − Q, MC = 0.

- Each q = 120/3 = **40**; Q = 80; P = **40**; each profit = 1,600
- Monopoly would produce 60 at P = 60; competition would give P = 0 here

steps.title: Solved: prisoner's dilemma
steps.body:
Two firms choose High or Low price. Payoffs (A, B): both High (10, 10); A Low, B High (15, 2); A High, B Low (2, 15); both Low (5, 5).

- For A, Low is better whatever B does (15 > 10, 5 > 2) — dominant; same for B
- Nash equilibrium: **(Low, Low)** with (5, 5), although (High, High) gives both more

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Nash equilibrium is always the best joint outcome.
- Using monopoly output for each Cournot firm.
- Assuming kinked demand explains how the price was set (it explains rigidity, not the level).
- Forgetting Bertrand's result depends on identical products and no capacity limits.

a.text: You and a rival café are the only two in town. Payoffs: both price high (₹10k each), you cut (₹15k vs ₹2k), both cut (₹5k each). The rival may cut. What do you do?

choices.label: Cut price
choices.feedback: Cutting is your dominant strategy in a one-shot game.

choices.label: Keep price high and hope
choices.feedback: If the rival cuts, you get only ₹2k.

a2.text: Compare your payoffs for each rival choice. Try again.

choices.label: Cut price
choices.feedback: Yes — better whatever the rival does.

b.text: Now you will compete every month for years. What might change?

choices.label: Cooperation (both high) can be sustained by tit-for-tat
choices.feedback: Repeated games can support cooperation — though explicit cartels are illegal under competition law.

choices.label: Nothing ever changes
choices.feedback: Repetition changes incentives; tacit cooperation becomes possible.

end.text: One-shot dilemmas push to the bad equilibrium; repeated interaction can sustain better outcomes.

quiz.q: In Cournot duopoly with P = a − bQ, each firm's output (MC = c):
quiz.why: In a Cournot duopoly, each firm's output is (a − c)/3b, from the two reaction functions. Total output is 2(a − c)/3b.

quiz.q: Bertrand with identical products leads to:
quiz.why: In Bertrand competition with identical products, firms undercut each other until price equals marginal cost: P = MC.
The kinked demand curve explains price rigidity in oligopoly. There is a gap in MR, so cost changes in that range do not change the price.

options: no player gains by unilateral deviation
quiz.why: Nash equilibrium is where no player gains by unilaterally changing strategy.

quiz.q: Cartels tend to be unstable because:
quiz.why: Cartels are unstable because each member can gain by cheating and selling more at the cartel price. That is the prisoner's dilemma logic.

questions.q: Under perfect competition, firms are:
questions.why: Under perfect competition there are many sellers, so each firm is a price taker.

questions.q: Profit-maximising rule for all firms:
questions.why: The general profit-maximising rule for any firm is MR = MC.

questions.q: A market with few interdependent sellers:
questions.why: A market with a few interdependent sellers is an oligopoly.

questions.q: Q = L^0.6 K^0.6 shows:
questions.why: The exponents add to 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2, which is more than 1, so it shows increasing returns to scale.

questions.q: TC = 40 + 6Q + Q². MC at Q = 5:
questions.why: MC is the derivative of TC: 6 + 2Q. At Q = 5, MC = 6 + 10 = 16.

questions.q: Long-run price in perfect competition equals:
questions.why: In the long run under perfect competition, entry and exit push price to the minimum of AC, so economic profit is zero.

questions.q: Assertion: A monopolist never operates on the inelastic part of demand. Reason: MR is negative where demand is inelastic.
questions.why: A monopolist sets MR = MC > 0. Since MR = P(1 − 1/|Ed|) is negative where demand is inelastic, it must operate where |Ed| > 1. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Monopolist: P = 60 − Q, MC = 20. Profit-maximising Q:
questions.why: MR = 60 − 2Q. Setting MR = MC gives 60 − 2Q = 20, so Q = 20.

questions.q: P = 30, AVC min = 35, AC min = 40. In the short run the firm should:
options: exit only in the long run but produce now
questions.why: P = 30 is below the minimum AVC of 35, so the firm can't even cover its variable costs. It should shut down in the short run.

questions.q: Case: Cournot duopoly, P = 90 − Q, MC = 30. Market price:
questions.why: In Cournot, each firm makes q = (90 − 30)/3 = 20. Total Q = 40, so P = 90 − 40 = 50.

questions.q: Monopoly P = 100 − 2Q, MC = 20: deadweight loss:
questions.why: MR = 100 − 4Q = 20 gives Q = 20, and P = 60. Competitive output is where P = MC: 100 − 2Q = 20, Q = 40. DWL = ½ × (40 − 20) × (60 − 20) = ½ × 20 × 40 = ₹400.

questions.q: Lerner index 0.25 implies |Ed| at the optimum:
questions.why: Lerner index = 1/|Ed|, so |Ed| = 1/0.25 = 4.

questions.q: A firm with TC = 100 + 10Q + Q² faces P = 30. Profit:
questions.why: MC = 10 + 2Q = 30 gives Q = 10. TR = 300 and TC = 100 + 100 + 100 = 300, so profit = 0.

questions.q: Two markets: |Ed| = 2 in A and 4 in B, same MC = ₹30. Prices (third-degree discrimination):
questions.why: Use P = MC/(1 − 1/|Ed|). In market A, 30/(1 − 1/2) = ₹60, and in market B, 30/(1 − 1/4) = ₹40. The less elastic market pays more.

questions.q: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma with a dominant strategy for each, the Nash equilibrium is:
questions.why: In a one-shot prisoner's dilemma, both players use their dominant strategy, so the Nash equilibrium is worse for both than mutual cooperation. It is Pareto-inferior.

Learners can analyse fiscal and monetary policy in IS–LM

scenes.text: Each quarter, newspapers report India's GDP growth. What exactly is being measured?
The value of all final goods and services produced in the country in a period — counted three equivalent ways.

steps.title: Aggregates
steps.body:
- **GDP** (market prices): value of final goods and services produced within the domestic territory
- Three methods: **value added** (output), **income** (wages + rent + interest + profit + mixed income), **expenditure**: GDP = C + I + G + (X − M)
- GNP = GDP + **net factor income from abroad (NFIA)**
- NNP = GNP − depreciation
- NNP at factor cost (national income) = NNP at market prices − **net indirect taxes** (indirect taxes − subsidies)
- Nominal vs real GDP; **GDP deflator** = nominal/real × 100
- Avoid double counting: count only final goods or value added; exclude transfer payments and second-hand sales (but include brokerage)

steps.title: Solved: from expenditure to national income
steps.body:
C 500, I 150, G 200, X 80, M 100, NFIA −10, depreciation 50, net indirect taxes 70.

- GDP_MP = 500 + 150 + 200 − 20 = **830**
- GNP_MP = 820; NNP_MP = 770
- NNP_FC (national income) = **700**

steps.title: Solved: value added
steps.body:
Farmer sells wheat ₹100 to a miller; miller sells flour ₹150 to a baker; baker sells bread ₹220.

- Value added: 100 + 50 + 70 = **₹220** = value of the final good
- Adding all sales (₹470) would double-count.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Including intermediate goods.
- Counting transfer payments (pensions, scholarships) in GDP.
- Subtracting subsidies instead of adding them when moving from MP to FC.
- Confusing GDP (territory) with GNP (residents).

activity.prompt: Order the steps from GDP at market prices to national income.
items: Start with GDP at market prices
Add net factor income from abroad → GNP_MP
Subtract net indirect taxes → NNP_FC (national income)

quiz.why: GNP = GDP + NFIA (net factor income from abroad), which is the income earned by residents abroad minus income of foreigners at home.
An old-age pension is a transfer payment, with no current production in exchange, so it is excluded from GDP.
GDP deflator = (nominal GDP ÷ real GDP) × 100 = (1,100 ÷ 1,000) × 100 = 110.
NNP at factor cost = NNP at market price − net indirect taxes (indirect taxes minus subsidies).
The value-added method counts only the value added at each stage, so it avoids double counting of intermediate goods.

scenes.text: The government spends ₹1,000 crore on a highway. Workers spend their wages, shopkeepers spend their earnings…
Total income rises by several times the original spending — the multiplier.

steps.title: The model
steps.body:
- Consumption C = a + bY; **MPC = b**, MPS = 1 − b
- Equilibrium: Y = C + I (+ G) ⇒ Y = (a + I + G)/(1 − b)
- **Investment/expenditure multiplier** k = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/MPS
- Lump-sum **tax multiplier** = −MPC/(1 − MPC)
- **Balanced budget multiplier** = 1
- **Paradox of thrift**: if everyone tries to save more, income falls and total saving may not rise

steps.title: Solved: fiscal multipliers
steps.body:
MPC = 0.75.

- Spending multiplier = 4; tax multiplier = −3
- ΔG = ΔT = 100 ⇒ ΔY = 400 − 300 = **100** (balanced budget multiplier 1)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 1/MPC instead of 1/(1 − MPC).
- Forgetting the minus sign on the tax multiplier.
- Ignoring leakages (taxes, imports) that reduce the multiplier in an open economy.
- Assuming the multiplier works instantly (it unfolds over rounds).

bands.text: Multiplier about 2–2.5: much of extra income leaks into saving.
Multiplier up to 10: spending circulates strongly.
Multiplier up to 20: very high (rare in practice, given taxes and imports).

quiz.why: Multiplier = 1/(1 − MPC) = 1/0.4 = 2.5.
The balanced budget multiplier is 1: an equal rise in G and T raises income by the same amount.
Extra income is either consumed or saved, so MPC + MPS = 1.
In equilibrium Y = C + I = 50 + 0.9Y + 100, so 0.1Y = 150 and Y = 1,500.

quiz.q: The paradox of thrift says higher saving desire can:
options: reduce income and leave total saving unchanged or lower
quiz.why: The paradox of thrift: if everyone tries to save more, demand and income fall. Total saving can stay the same or even fall.

lessons.title: IS–LM: goods and money market equilibrium

scenes.text: In the same month, the government raises spending and the RBI considers a rate change.
IS–LM shows how goods and money markets jointly decide output and interest rates.

steps.title: The curves
steps.body:
- **IS** (goods market): Y = C(Y − T) + I(r) + G — downward sloping in (Y, r)
- **LM** (money market): M/P = L(Y, r), money demand rising with Y and falling with r — upward sloping
- Expansionary fiscal policy shifts IS right ⇒ Y ↑, r ↑ (some **crowding out**)
- Expansionary monetary policy shifts LM right ⇒ Y ↑, r ↓
- **Liquidity trap** (flat LM): monetary policy weak, fiscal policy strong; **vertical LM** (classical): fiscal policy fully crowded out

steps.title: Solved: fiscal expansion
steps.body:
G rises by 30 ⇒ IS: Y = 2,650 − 100r.

- 2,650 − 100r = 2,000 + 50r ⇒ r = 4.33, Y ≈ 2,217
- Simple multiplier would give ΔY = 5 × 30 = 150; actual ΔY ≈ 50 — the rest is **crowded out** by the higher interest rate

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Shifting LM for fiscal policy or IS for monetary policy.
- Forgetting that a higher price level shifts LM left (lower real balances).
- Treating crowding out as complete in all cases.
- Mixing up the axes (r vertical, Y horizontal).

activity.prompt: Which curve shifts, and which way?

quiz.q: IS curve represents equilibrium in the:
quiz.why: The IS curve shows equilibrium in the goods market, where investment equals saving.
Expansionary monetary policy shifts the LM curve right. Income rises and the interest rate falls.

quiz.q: In a liquidity trap, the LM curve is:
quiz.why: In a liquidity trap, money demand is infinitely elastic at a low interest rate, so the LM curve is horizontal.

quiz.q: Crowding out occurs because fiscal expansion:
quiz.why: Fiscal expansion raises the interest rate, which reduces private investment. This is crowding out.

quiz.q: A higher price level shifts LM:
quiz.why: A higher price level lowers real money balances, so the LM curve shifts left.

lessons.title: Aggregate demand, aggregate supply and the Phillips curve

scenes.text: Global crude prices jump. Transport, fertiliser and plastics all get costlier.
Prices rise and output falls together — a supply shock in the AD–AS model.

steps.title: AD–AS
steps.body:
- **AD** slopes down (real-balance, interest-rate and exchange-rate effects)
- **SRAS** slopes up (sticky wages/prices); **LRAS** vertical at potential output
- Demand shock (AD right): output and prices up in the short run
- Supply shock (SRAS left): **stagflation** — prices up, output down
- **Phillips curve**: short-run inverse relation between inflation and unemployment; long run vertical at the natural rate (expectations-augmented view)
- Fisher equation: nominal interest ≈ real interest + expected inflation

steps.title: Solved: classify the shock
steps.body:
- Large tax cut → AD right → higher output and prices (short run)
- Bad monsoon raises food prices → SRAS left → higher prices, lower output
- Productivity gain from digitisation → SRAS and LRAS right → more output, lower prices

steps.title: Solved: Fisher
steps.body:
A bank FD offers 7% when expected inflation is 5%.

- Real return ≈ 7 − 5 = **2%**
- If inflation turns out 8%, the real return is about −1%

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating the short-run Phillips trade-off as permanent.
- Saying supply shocks shift AD.
- Forgetting that LRAS is vertical (output determined by resources and technology).
- Using nominal returns to judge savings without subtracting inflation.

activity.prompt: Match the event to its effect in AD–AS.

quiz.why: Stagflation (stagnation with inflation) comes from an adverse supply shock, when the short-run aggregate supply curve shifts left.
The long-run Phillips curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment, so there is no permanent trade-off between inflation and unemployment.

quiz.q: Nominal rate 9%, expected inflation 4%. Real rate ≈
quiz.why: By the Fisher equation, real rate ≈ nominal − expected inflation = 9% − 4% = 5%.
Long-run aggregate supply depends on resources and technology, not on the price level or money supply.

quiz.q: A demand-pull inflation is caused by:
quiz.why: Demand-pull inflation is caused by aggregate demand rising faster than the economy's supply of goods.

questions.q: GDP measures production:
questions.why: GDP measures production within the country's domestic territory, whoever produces it. GNP is by citizens anywhere.

questions.q: Multiplier formula:
questions.why: The Keynesian multiplier is 1/(1 − MPC).

questions.q: LM curve slopes:
questions.why: The LM curve slopes upward, because higher income raises money demand and needs a higher interest rate for money market equilibrium.

questions.q: GDP_MP 1,000; depreciation 80; NFIA 20; NIT 100. National income:
questions.why: National income (NNP at factor cost) = GDP at market price + NFIA − depreciation − net indirect taxes = 1,000 + 20 − 80 − 100 = 840.

questions.q: MPS = 0.25. Multiplier:
questions.why: Multiplier = 1/MPS = 1/0.25 = 4.

questions.q: Expansionary fiscal policy in IS–LM raises:
questions.why: Expansionary fiscal policy shifts IS right, raising both income Y and the interest rate r.

questions.q: Assertion: Fiscal policy is most effective in a liquidity trap. Reason: A flat LM means no rise in interest rates and no crowding out.
questions.why: In a liquidity trap, LM is flat, so fiscal expansion doesn't raise interest rates and doesn't crowd out investment. So both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: C = 200 + 0.75Y, I = 100, G = 100. Equilibrium Y:
Tax multiplier when MPC = 0.9:
questions.why: The tax multiplier = −MPC/(1 − MPC) = −0.9/0.1 = −9.

questions.q: Case: IS Y = 1,200 − 40r; LM Y = 800 + 60r. Equilibrium r and Y:
Real GDP rose 6% and the GDP deflator 4%. Nominal GDP growth ≈
questions.why: Nominal GDP growth ≈ real growth + inflation = 6% + 4% = 10% (approximately).

questions.q: Government raises G and T by ₹500 crore each. Change in Y (simple model):
questions.why: With the balanced budget multiplier equal to 1, an equal rise in G and T of ₹500 crore raises Y by ₹500 crore.

questions.q: IS: Y = 2,500 − 100r; LM: Y = 2,000 + 50r. If money supply rises so LM becomes Y = 2,150 + 50r, new Y:
With income tax rate t and MPC b, the multiplier becomes:
questions.why: With an income tax, only b(1 − t) of extra income is spent, so the multiplier is 1/(1 − b(1 − t)). Taxes act as another leakage.

courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Money supply measures and credit creation, RBI monetary policy tools and the inflation-targeting framework, budget deficits and fiscal policy, and the balance of payments with exchange rates.
outcomes: Learners can compute money multipliers and explain RBI tools
Learners can describe India's inflation-targeting framework
Learners can compute fiscal, revenue and primary deficits
Learners can read balance-of-payments accounts and exchange-rate movements

scenes.text: Manav deposits ₹10,000 in a bank. The bank lends most of it; the borrower's spending becomes someone else's deposit…
Banks create deposit money through this chain, limited by reserve requirements.

steps.title: Measures and multiplier
steps.body:
- **Reserve money (M0)**: currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI
- **M1** (narrow money): currency with the public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with RBI
- **M3** (broad money): M1 + time deposits with banks
- Simple deposit multiplier = 1/required reserve ratio
- With a currency ratio c and reserve ratio r: money multiplier = (1 + c)/(c + r)

steps.title: Solved: credit creation
steps.body:
New deposit ₹10,000; reserve ratio 10%; no cash leakage.

- Multiplier = 1/0.10 = 10
- Total deposits = **₹1,00,000**; new loans = ₹90,000

steps.title: Solved: with currency leakage
steps.body:
c = 0.2, r = 0.1.

- m = 1.2/0.3 = **4**
- An increase in reserve money of ₹1,000 crore raises money supply by about ₹4,000 crore

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying banks lend 100% of deposits.
- Ignoring currency leakage in real-world multipliers.
- Treating M3 as narrower than M1.
- Confusing reserve money with money supply.

activity.prompt: If the required reserve ratio is 5% and there is no currency leakage, what is the simple deposit multiplier?

quiz.why: In India, M3 is the broad money measure, as it includes time deposits with banks. M1 is narrow money.
The simple deposit multiplier is 1/r = 1/0.2 = 5.
Reserve money is also called high-powered money, because it is the base on which the money supply is built.

quiz.q: Higher currency holding by the public makes the multiplier:
quiz.why: When the public holds more currency, less money returns to banks as deposits. This leakage reduces the amount banks can lend, so the money multiplier gets smaller.
M1 is narrow money: currency with the public plus demand deposits with banks (and other deposits with the RBI). Time deposits are in the broader measure.

scenes.text: TV anchors announce the Monetary Policy Committee's decision on the repo rate.
Home-loan EMIs, FD rates and business borrowing all respond. How?

steps.title: Framework and tools
steps.body:
- **Flexible inflation targeting** (RBI Act amended 2016): CPI inflation target **4%** with a band of **2–6%**
- **Monetary Policy Committee**: 6 members (3 from RBI including the Governor, 3 external); decides the policy repo rate
- Tools: **repo rate** (RBI lends to banks), **Standing Deposit Facility** (floor of the corridor, introduced 2022), **Marginal Standing Facility** (ceiling), reverse repo, **CRR**, **SLR**, open market operations
- Contractionary policy: raise repo/CRR, sell bonds ⇒ credit costlier ⇒ demand and inflation cool
- Inflation types: demand-pull, cost-push, built-in; measures: CPI (target measure), WPI
- Quantity theory: MV = PY

steps.title: Solved: quantity theory
steps.body:
M grows 10%, V constant, real output grows 6%.

- %ΔP ≈ %ΔM + %ΔV − %ΔY = 10 + 0 − 6 = **4% inflation**

steps.title: Solved: policy reading
steps.body:
CPI inflation is 6.8% and rising, growth is strong.

- Above the 6% upper band ⇒ the MPC is likely to **tighten** (raise the repo rate or withdraw liquidity)
- Effect chain: bank lending rates ↑ → borrowing ↓ → demand ↓ → inflation ↓ (with lags)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the repo rate is the rate RBI pays banks (that is the SDF/reverse repo).
- Treating WPI as the official target measure (it is CPI).
- Expecting instant effects (monetary policy acts with lags).
- Confusing CRR (cash with RBI) with SLR (liquid assets held by banks themselves).

activity.prompt: Expansionary or contractionary?

quiz.why: India's flexible inflation targeting framework (since 2016) sets a CPI target of 4%, with a tolerance band of 2–6%.
The Monetary Policy Committee has 6 members: 3 from the RBI and 3 external members.

quiz.q: Repo rate is the rate at which:
quiz.why: The repo rate is the rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to banks. It is the main policy rate.
Raising the CRR makes banks keep more reserves with the RBI. They have less to lend, so it reduces their lending capacity.

quiz.q: MV = PY: if M rises 8%, Y 5%, V constant, inflation ≈
quiz.why: From MV = PY with V constant, inflation ≈ money growth − real output growth = 8% − 5% = 3%.

scenes.text: On 1 February, the Finance Minister presents the Union Budget. Headlines focus on the 'fiscal deficit'.
What exactly is it, and how is it different from the revenue and primary deficits?

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Revenue receipts**: tax + non-tax revenue; **capital receipts**: borrowings, loan recoveries, disinvestment
- **Revenue deficit** = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts
- **Fiscal deficit** = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) = borrowing requirement
- **Primary deficit** = fiscal deficit − interest payments
- Direct taxes (income tax, corporation tax) vs indirect (GST, customs)
- Fiscal discipline law: **FRBM Act, 2003**
- Fiscal policy tools: spending, taxation, transfers; automatic stabilisers

steps.title: Solved: three deficits
steps.body:
Revenue receipts 25; non-debt capital receipts 1; revenue expenditure 35; capital expenditure 10; interest payments 10 (₹ lakh crore).

- Revenue deficit = 35 − 25 = **10**
- Fiscal deficit = 45 − 26 = **19**
- Primary deficit = 19 − 10 = **9**

steps.title: Solved: as % of GDP
steps.body: Fiscal deficit ₹16 lakh crore; GDP ₹320 lakh crore ⇒ **5% of GDP**. A falling ratio can come from a smaller deficit or faster GDP growth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting borrowings as revenue receipts.
- Subtracting interest from revenue deficit (it is subtracted from fiscal deficit for primary deficit).
- Calling GST a direct tax.
- Assuming all deficits are harmful (borrowing for productive capital spending can raise growth).

activity.prompt: Fiscal deficit is ₹18 lakh crore and interest payments are ₹11 lakh crore. Primary deficit (₹ lakh crore)?

quiz.why: The fiscal deficit is total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowing. So it is the government's total borrowing requirement.
Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments. It shows borrowing needed for current spending, excluding the cost of past debt.
Market borrowing is a capital receipt, because it creates a liability. GST, income tax and PSU dividends are revenue receipts.
The FRBM (Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management) Act was enacted in 2003 to promote fiscal discipline.
Corporation tax is a direct tax, as it is levied on company income and cannot be passed on easily.

lessons.title: Balance of payments and exchange rates

scenes.text: The rupee slips against the dollar; importers worry, exporters smile.
Behind it: flows of goods, services, remittances and capital recorded in the balance of payments.

steps.title: BoP structure
steps.body:
- **Current account**: merchandise trade, services (invisibles), primary income, transfers (remittances)
- **Capital (and financial) account**: FDI, portfolio investment, loans, banking capital
- Changes in **foreign exchange reserves** balance the accounts
- India often runs a trade deficit in goods offset partly by surpluses in services and remittances
- **Exchange rate**: price of one currency in terms of another; depreciation of the rupee (₹ per $ rises) makes exports cheaper and imports dearer
- India moved to a market-determined exchange rate in 1993 (managed float); **PPP** theory links exchange rates to price levels

steps.title: Solved: current account
steps.body:
Goods exports 450, goods imports 700, net services +160, net transfers +110, net primary income −40 ($ billion).

- Trade balance = −250
- Current account = −250 + 160 + 110 − 40 = **−20** (deficit)

steps.title: Solved: depreciation
steps.body:
Rupee moves from ₹80/$ to ₹84/$.

- Rupee **depreciates** by 5%; a $100 import now costs ₹8,400 instead of ₹8,000
- An exporter earning $100 receives ₹400 more

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying '₹ per $ rose' means the rupee appreciated.
- Placing remittances in the capital account (they are current transfers).
- Thinking BoP 'balance' means no deficit anywhere (accounts sum to zero by construction).
- Confusing devaluation (policy act under fixed rates) with depreciation (market movement).

activity.prompt: Current account or capital/financial account?

quiz.why: Remittances are current transfers, so they are recorded in the current account of the balance of payments.

quiz.q: ₹/$ rising from 82 to 86 means the rupee has:
quiz.why: When ₹/$ rises from 82 to 86, it takes more rupees to buy a dollar. So the rupee has depreciated.
FDI is an investment flow, so it appears in the financial (capital) account, not the current account.
Depreciation makes exports cheaper for foreign buyers, in terms of their currency. So exports tend to rise.

quiz.q: India adopted a market-determined exchange rate in:
quiz.why: India moved to a market-determined exchange rate in 1993, after the transition (LERMS) that followed the 1991 reforms.

questions.q: Inflation target measure in India:
questions.why: The RBI's inflation target is measured using the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

questions.q: Revenue deficit =
questions.why: Revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.

questions.q: Remittances belong to the:
questions.why: Remittances are current transfers, so they belong to the current account.

questions.q: Simple multiplier with CRR 4% (no leakages):
questions.why: The simple deposit multiplier is 1/reserve ratio = 1/0.04 = 25.

questions.q: Contractionary monetary tool:
questions.why: Raising the repo rate makes borrowing dearer and reduces credit, so it is a contractionary (tightening) tool. Cutting CRR or SLR and buying bonds expand money supply.

questions.q: Fiscal deficit 20, interest 12. Primary deficit:
questions.why: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments = 20 − 12 = 8.

questions.q: Assertion: OMO purchases increase money supply. Reason: RBI pays banks for bonds, raising their reserves.
questions.why: When the RBI buys bonds under OMO, it pays banks, which raises their reserves and so the money supply. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: c = 0.25, r = 0.05. Money multiplier:
The rupee price of one dollar rises from ₹75 to ₹90. By what percentage has the rupee price of the dollar risen?
questions.why: The rupee price of the dollar rose from 75 to 90, so the rise is 15 ÷ 75 = 20%.

questions.q: Case: Exports 300, imports 450, net invisibles +120. Current account balance:
questions.why: Trade balance = 300 − 450 = −150. Adding net invisibles of +120 gives a current account balance of −30 (a deficit).

questions.q: M grows 12%, V falls 2%, real GDP grows 6%. Inflation ≈
questions.why: From MV = PY: inflation ≈ M growth + V growth − real GDP growth = 12 − 2 − 6 = 4%.

questions.q: Total expenditure 50, revenue receipts 30, non-debt capital receipts 2, interest 9. Fiscal and primary deficits:
questions.why: Fiscal deficit = total expenditure − (revenue receipts + non-debt capital receipts) = 50 − 32 = 18. Primary deficit = 18 − 9 = 9.

questions.q: If CPI inflation is 1.5% for several quarters, the RBI framework would view it as:
options: below the tolerance band (failure condition if sustained)
questions.why: The RBI's tolerance band is 2–6%. CPI inflation of 1.5% for several quarters is below the band, and sustained for long it counts as a failure condition.

questions.q: Under flexible exchange rates, a large inflow of FPI tends to:
questions.why: A large inflow of foreign portfolio investment raises demand for rupees. Under flexible exchange rates, this appreciates the rupee.

questions.q: Which reduces primary deficit but not fiscal deficit?
options: higher interest payments with equal cut elsewhere
questions.why: If interest payments rise and an equal amount is cut elsewhere, the fiscal deficit doesn't change. But interest is a bigger part of it, so primary deficit (FD − interest) falls.

courses.title: Indian Economy & Development · planning, reforms, poverty
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Growth versus development and the HDI, planning from the Five-Year Plans to NITI Aayog, the 1991 reforms and later structural changes, and poverty, inequality and employment.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish growth and development and compute an HDI
Learners can outline India's planning history
Learners can explain the 1991 crisis and LPG reforms
Learners can interpret Lorenz curves, Gini coefficients and poverty measures

scenes.text: Two states have similar income per head, but one has far longer life expectancy and higher literacy.
Development is more than income — the Human Development Index captures that.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Growth**: rise in real output (GDP/GNP) — quantitative
- **Development**: improvement in well-being, capabilities and freedoms — qualitative (Amartya Sen's capability approach)
- **HDI** (UNDP, first published 1990): geometric mean of three dimension indices — **health** (life expectancy), **education** (mean and expected years of schooling), **standard of living** (GNI per capita, PPP, log)
- Dimension index = (actual − minimum)/(maximum − minimum)
- Related: inequality-adjusted HDI, gender indices, multidimensional poverty index

steps.title: Solved: HDI from indices
steps.body:
Health 0.80, education 0.60, income 0.70.

- HDI = (0.80 × 0.60 × 0.70)^(1/3) = (0.336)^(1/3) ≈ **0.695**
- An arithmetic mean (0.70) would hide imbalance; the geometric mean penalises low scores in any one dimension

steps.title: Solved: a dimension index
steps.body:
Life expectancy 70 years; goalposts 20 and 85.

- Health index = (70 − 20)/(85 − 20) = 50/65 ≈ **0.769**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating growth with development.
- Using arithmetic instead of geometric mean for the current HDI.
- Forgetting HDI uses GNI (not GDP) per capita in PPP terms.
- Treating HDI as a complete welfare measure (it omits inequality, environment, etc.).

activity.prompt: Compute the HDI (geometric mean) for indices 0.9, 0.8 and 0.5. Give 3 decimals.

quiz.why: The Human Development Index is published by the UNDP in its Human Development Report.
HDI has three dimensions: health (life expectancy), education, and standard of living (income).

quiz.q: The capability approach is associated with:
quiz.why: The capability approach, 'development as freedom', is associated with Amartya Sen.
Since 2010, HDI combines its three dimension indices using the geometric mean. This penalises uneven achievement.
Economic growth is mainly quantitative: an increase in output. Development is broader and qualitative.

lessons.title: Planning: Five-Year Plans to NITI Aayog

scenes.text: In the 1950s India built steel plants at Bhilai, Rourkela and Durgapur under its plans.
In the 1960s, high-yielding seeds transformed Punjab's fields. Both were planned choices.

steps.title: Milestones
steps.body:
- **Planning Commission** set up in 1950
- **First Plan (1951–56)**: agriculture and irrigation; based on a Harrod–Domar-type model
- **Second Plan (1956–61)**: heavy industry; **Mahalanobis model**
- Plan holidays 1966–69 after war and drought
- **Green Revolution** from the mid-1960s: HYV seeds, fertilisers, irrigation — especially wheat in Punjab, Haryana, western UP
- **Bank nationalisation**: 14 banks in 1969, 6 more in 1980
- **Twelfth Plan (2012–17)** was the last Five-Year Plan
- **NITI Aayog** replaced the Planning Commission on **1 January 2015** — a policy think-tank promoting cooperative federalism

steps.title: Solved: Harrod–Domar
steps.body:
Growth g = s/v (saving rate / capital–output ratio).

- s = 20%, v = 4 ⇒ g = **5%**
- To grow 8% with v = 4 needs s = 32%

steps.title: Solved: evaluate the Green Revolution
steps.body:
Gains: food self-sufficiency, higher wheat and rice yields, fewer imports.
Costs: regional and crop inequality, groundwater depletion, soil degradation, heavy fertiliser use. A balanced answer cites both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the Mahalanobis model in the First Plan.
- Saying NITI Aayog makes Five-Year Plans (it does not).
- Giving 1991 as the year of bank nationalisation.
- Treating the Green Revolution as uniformly beneficial.

activity.prompt: Order these events in India's economic history.

events.text: NITI Aayog replaces the Planning Commission

quiz.why: The Second Five-Year Plan, based on the Mahalanobis model, emphasised heavy industry.

quiz.q: NITI Aayog was set up in:
quiz.why: NITI Aayog was set up on 1 January 2015, replacing the Planning Commission.
In the Harrod–Domar model, growth g = s/v = 24% ÷ 3 = 8%.
India nationalised its first set of 14 major banks in 1969.
The Green Revolution, with high-yielding varieties, mainly boosted wheat production, and later rice.

scenes.text: In 1991, India pledged gold reserves abroad to raise emergency foreign exchange.
The crisis triggered sweeping reforms — liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation.

steps.title: Crisis and response
steps.body:
**Causes of the 1991 crisis**: high fiscal deficits, a large current account deficit, rising external debt, the Gulf War oil-price spike and fall in remittances; foreign exchange reserves fell to only a few weeks of imports.

**Reforms (LPG)**:
- Industrial delicensing; reduced reservation for the public sector
- Rupee devaluation (July 1991) and move toward market-determined exchange rate
- Trade liberalisation: tariff cuts, removal of quantitative restrictions
- FDI liberalisation; disinvestment in public enterprises
- Financial sector reforms (Narasimham Committee), capital market regulator SEBI given statutory powers (1992)

**Later structural changes**: Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (2016), GST (2017), inflation targeting (2016), digital public infrastructure (Aadhaar, UPI)

steps.title: Solved: link cause and reform
steps.body:
- Current account crisis → devaluation, export promotion, FDI opening
- Fiscal crisis → expenditure control, tax reform

steps.title: Solved: evaluating outcomes
steps.body: After 1991: faster average growth, rise of services/IT exports, larger reserves and foreign investment. Critiques: jobless growth phases, agrarian distress, regional inequality. A strong answer weighs evidence on both sides.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying reforms began with GST.
- Confusing devaluation (1991) with demonetisation (2016).
- Listing reforms without linking them to causes of the crisis.
- Treating 'privatisation' as only selling PSUs (it also means opening sectors to private firms).

activity.prompt: Match each reform to its main purpose.
pairs: Speed up resolution of bad loans

quiz.why: LPG stands for liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation, the reform package that began in 1991.
The 1991 crisis was mainly a balance of payments crisis, as foreign exchange reserves had collapsed.
The Narasimham Committee gave reports on banking reforms in 1991 and 1998.
SEBI was given statutory powers by the SEBI Act of 1992.

quiz.q: Which is NOT part of the 1991 package?
quiz.why: GST is not part of the 1991 package, since it was introduced in 2017. Delicensing, trade liberalisation and devaluation were part of 1991.

scenes.text: Two reports on the same year give different poverty numbers.
They use different poverty lines and methods. Understanding measurement is half the debate.

steps.title: Measures
steps.body:
- **Income/consumption poverty**: share of people below a poverty line (expert groups such as Tendulkar and Rangarajan proposed different lines)
- **Multidimensional poverty** (MPI): deprivations in health, education and living standards; NITI Aayog publishes a national MPI
- **Lorenz curve**: cumulative % of income vs cumulative % of population; **Gini coefficient** = area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve ÷ total area under the equality line (0 = equal, 1 = maximal inequality)
- **Unemployment types**: open, disguised (marginal product ≈ 0, common in agriculture), seasonal, structural, frictional; data from the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS)
- **Demographic dividend**: a large working-age share can raise growth if jobs and skills keep pace

steps.title: Solved: disguised unemployment
steps.body: A family farm needs 4 workers but 6 family members work on it. Removing 2 leaves output unchanged ⇒ **2 are disguisedly unemployed** (their marginal product is zero).

steps.title: Common mistakes

quiz.why: Workers whose marginal product is zero are in disguised unemployment: they look employed but removing them would not reduce output.
India's main labour force survey is the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS).

quiz.q: A Lorenz curve further from the diagonal shows:
quiz.why: A Lorenz curve further from the diagonal means a larger gap from perfect equality, so more inequality.

questions.q: NITI Aayog replaced the:

questions.q: Higher Gini means:

questions.q: Rupee was devalued in:

questions.why: Harrod–Domar: g = s/v, so s = g × v = 7% × 5 = 35%.

questions.why: HDI is the geometric mean: (0.5 × 0.8 × 0.8)^(1/3) = 0.32^(1/3) ≈ 0.684. The simple average would give 0.70.

questions.why: Health index = (actual − minimum) ÷ (maximum − minimum) = (75 − 20) ÷ (85 − 20) = 55/65 ≈ 0.846.

questions.why: If health and education lag behind income growth, relative to other countries, the HDI rank can fall even as GDP grows. HDI does include income.

questions.q: The demographic dividend turns into a burden when:
options: job creation and skills fail to absorb the working-age population
questions.why: The demographic dividend becomes a burden when job creation and skills can't absorb the working-age population. Then unemployment rises.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- Ed = %ΔQ/%ΔP; arc with averages; point (dQ/dP)(P/Q); MR = P(1 − 1/|Ed|)
- Equi-marginal MUx/Px = MUy/Py; tangency MRS = Px/Py; Cobb–Douglas x = aM/Px
- CS = ½ × Q × (intercept − P) for linear demand
- Returns to scale: α + β vs 1
- MC cuts AVC and AC at minima
- PC: P = MC; shutdown P < min AVC; LR P = min AC
- Monopoly: MR = MC; Lerner = 1/|Ed|; DWL triangle
- Cournot: q = (a − c)/3b each

steps.body: Demand Q = 120 − 3P. At P = 30, Q = 30, Ed = −3 × 30/30 = −3 (elastic) ⇒ a price **cut** raises revenue. Revenue-maximising price is the midpoint P = 20.

The HDI is the geometric mean of the three indices. If all are 0.9, the HDI is 0.9, not their sum or product.

questions.q: MC cuts AC at:

questions.q: Gini ranges between:
questions.why: The Gini coefficient is a ratio of areas, so it ranges from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality).

courses.title: Psychology I · schools, brain, perception, learning
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: The history and methods of psychology, biological bases of behaviour, sensation and perception, and classical, operant and observational learning.
outcomes: Learners can describe the major schools and research methods
Learners can relate brain regions and neurotransmitters to functions
Learners can apply Weber's law and Gestalt principles
Learners can analyse behaviour with conditioning and observational learning

scenes.text: Hostel friends argue: Ali says music helps him study; Bina says it distracts her.
A psychologist would test it: random groups, same test, music vs silence — an experiment.

steps.title: Schools
steps.body:
- **Structuralism** (Wilhelm Wundt; first psychology laboratory, Leipzig, 1879): elements of conscious experience via introspection
- **Functionalism** (William James): purpose of mental processes
- **Psychoanalysis** (Sigmund Freud): unconscious motives
- **Behaviourism** (John B. Watson, B. F. Skinner): observable behaviour
- **Humanistic** (Abraham Maslow, Carl Rogers): growth and self-actualisation
- **Cognitive**: memory, thinking, information processing; today also biological, evolutionary and cultural perspectives

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- **Experiment**: manipulate an independent variable (IV), measure a dependent variable (DV), control extraneous variables, random assignment ⇒ cause and effect
- **Correlation**: relationship (r from −1 to +1) — not causation
- Surveys, case studies, naturalistic observation, psychological tests (reliability and validity)
- **Ethics**: informed consent, confidentiality, right to withdraw, debriefing, protection from harm

steps.title: Solved: name the variables
steps.body:
Study: does caffeine improve reaction time?

- IV = caffeine dose; DV = reaction time
- Control: same time of day, same test, placebo group (double-blind)
- Random assignment rules out pre-existing differences

steps.title: Solved: correlation ≠ causation
steps.body:
r = +0.6 between hours of social media and loneliness.

- Possible: social media → loneliness; loneliness → more social media; or a third variable (e.g. stress) causes both
- Only an experiment or strong longitudinal design can test cause

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every study an 'experiment'.
- Treating a strong correlation as proof of cause.
- Confusing reliability (consistency) with validity (measures what it claims).
- Forgetting ethics, especially consent and debriefing.

activity.prompt: Match the school to its key figure.

quiz.q: First psychology laboratory (1879) was founded by:
quiz.why: Wilhelm Wundt founded the first psychology laboratory, in Leipzig in 1879.

quiz.q: In an experiment, the variable manipulated is the:
quiz.why: In an experiment, the variable that the researcher manipulates is the independent variable (IV). The DV is what is measured.
A correlation of r = −0.8 is close to −1, so it shows a strong negative relationship. Correlation does not show causation.
Humanistic psychology emphasises personal growth and self-actualisation, as in Maslow and Rogers.

quiz.q: Consistency of a test over time is its:
quiz.why: Consistency of a test over time is its reliability (test–retest). Validity means it measures what it should.

scenes.text: In 1848, a railway foreman survived an iron rod passing through his frontal lobe.
Friends said he was 'no longer Gage' — impulsive and unreliable. The frontal lobe shapes planning and self-control.

steps.title: Neurons and neurotransmitters
steps.body:
- Neuron: dendrites (receive), cell body, axon (conducts), myelin sheath (speeds conduction), terminal buttons
- Action potential is all-or-none; signals cross the **synapse** chemically
- Neurotransmitters: **acetylcholine** (muscle action, memory), **dopamine** (reward, movement), **serotonin** (mood, sleep), **GABA** (main inhibitory), **glutamate** (main excitatory), **norepinephrine** (arousal)

steps.title: Brain regions
steps.body:
- **Frontal lobe**: planning, decision-making, personality; motor cortex; **Broca's area** (speech production, usually left)
- **Parietal**: touch and body sense (somatosensory cortex)
- **Temporal**: hearing; **Wernicke's area** (language comprehension)
- **Occipital**: vision
- Limbic system: **hippocampus** (forming new memories), **amygdala** (fear, emotion), **hypothalamus** (hunger, temperature, hormones)
- Cerebellum: balance and coordination; brainstem: breathing and heart rate

steps.title: Solved: brain-damage cases
steps.body:
- A patient understands speech but speaks haltingly → **Broca's area**
- Fluent but meaningless speech, poor comprehension → **Wernicke's area**
- Cannot form new long-term memories after surgery (patient H.M., 1953) → **hippocampus**

steps.title: Solved: transmitter links
steps.body:
- Loss of dopamine neurons in the substantia nigra → movement problems in **Parkinson's disease**
- Many antidepressants act on **serotonin** reuptake
- Anti-anxiety drugs often enhance **GABA**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping Broca's (production) and Wernicke's (comprehension).
- Believing 'we use only 10% of our brain' (a myth).
- Treating left/right-brained personalities as scientific (hemispheres specialise but cooperate).
- Saying neurotransmitters have only one function each.

activity.prompt: Match the brain region to its function.

quiz.why: GABA is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter. It reduces neuron firing.
The myelin sheath insulates axons and speeds up the conduction of nerve impulses.

quiz.q: Fluent but meaningless speech suggests damage to:
quiz.why: Fluent but meaningless speech (Wernicke's aphasia) suggests damage to Wernicke's area, which is for language comprehension. Broca's damage causes halting speech.
The hypothalamus regulates hunger, thirst and body temperature, maintaining homeostasis.
Parkinson's disease involves loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra.

scenes.text: One extra spoon of sugar is obvious in a small cup but barely noticed in a big jug.
Weber's law: what we notice depends on the proportion of change, not the absolute amount.

steps.title: Sensation
steps.body:
- **Absolute threshold**: minimum stimulus detected 50% of the time
- **Difference threshold (JND)**: smallest detectable change; **Weber's law**: ΔI/I = k (constant fraction)
- Sensory adaptation: reduced sensitivity to constant stimuli
- Signal detection theory: detection depends on sensitivity and decision criteria

steps.title: Perception
steps.body:
- **Gestalt principles**: figure–ground, proximity, similarity, closure, continuity
- **Depth cues**: binocular (retinal disparity, convergence) and monocular (linear perspective, relative size, interposition, texture gradient)
- **Perceptual constancy**: size, shape, colour
- Top-down (expectation-driven) vs bottom-up (data-driven) processing; perceptual set
- Illusions (Müller-Lyer) show perception is constructive

steps.title: Solved: Weber's law
steps.body:
For weight, k ≈ 0.02. Holding 500 g, what change is just noticeable?

- ΔI = 0.02 × 500 = **10 g**
- Holding 2 kg: ΔI = 40 g

steps.title: Solved: name the cue
steps.body:
- Railway tracks appear to converge in the distance → **linear perspective**
- A car partly hidden behind a tree seems farther → **interposition**
- Your eyes turning inward to look at a near object → **convergence** (binocular)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating sensation and perception as the same (detection vs interpretation).
- Calling relative size a binocular cue.
- Thinking JND is a fixed amount rather than a proportion.
- Assuming illusions mean the senses are 'broken' (they reveal normal processing rules).

activity.prompt: Binocular or monocular depth cue?

quiz.q: Weber's law states that the JND is:
options: a constant proportion of the stimulus
quiz.why: Weber's law says the just noticeable difference (JND) is a constant proportion of the original stimulus: ΔI/I = k.

quiz.q: Seeing a complete circle from a broken outline illustrates:
quiz.why: Seeing a complete circle from a broken outline is the Gestalt principle of closure: the mind fills in the gaps.

quiz.q: A door seen at an angle still looks rectangular:
quiz.why: A door seen at an angle still looks rectangular because of shape constancy, even though its retinal image changes.

quiz.q: Not noticing a fridge hum after a while:
quiz.why: Not noticing a constant stimulus, like a fridge hum, after a while is sensory adaptation.

quiz.q: k = 0.1 for loudness; base level 60 units. JND:
quiz.why: By Weber's law, JND = k × base = 0.1 × 60 = 6 units.

scenes.text: Kiran grabs her phone at the ping, even when it is someone else's phone.
The ping (once neutral) now triggers anticipation — Pavlov would call it a conditioned stimulus. And unpredictable likes keep her checking — a variable-ratio schedule.

steps.title: Classical conditioning (Pavlov)
steps.body:
- Unconditioned stimulus (UCS: food) → unconditioned response (UCR: salivation)
- Neutral stimulus (bell) paired with UCS becomes a **conditioned stimulus (CS)** → **conditioned response (CR)**
- Extinction (CS without UCS), spontaneous recovery, generalisation, discrimination
- Watson and Rayner's 'Little Albert' study (1920) — conditioned fear; ethically unacceptable today

steps.title: Operant and observational learning
steps.body:
- **Operant** (Skinner): behaviour shaped by consequences
- **Positive reinforcement** (add pleasant), **negative reinforcement** (remove unpleasant) — both increase behaviour; **punishment** decreases it
- Schedules: fixed ratio, variable ratio (most resistant to extinction), fixed interval, variable interval
- **Observational learning** (Albert Bandura; Bobo doll studies, early 1960s): attention, retention, reproduction, motivation; vicarious reinforcement

steps.title: Solved: identify the parts
steps.body:
A child is stung by a bee and later fears all buzzing sounds.

- UCS = sting; UCR = pain/fear
- CS = buzzing; CR = fear of buzzing
- Fear of a buzzing trimmer too → **generalisation**

steps.title: Solved: reinforcement or punishment?
steps.body:
- Seat-belt alarm stops when you buckle up → **negative reinforcement** (buckling increases)
- Extra screen time for finishing homework → **positive reinforcement**
- Losing phone time for rudeness → **negative punishment** (removing something pleasant)

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling negative reinforcement 'punishment'.
- Mixing classical (involuntary responses) with operant (voluntary behaviour).
- Thinking extinction erases learning (spontaneous recovery shows it doesn't).
- Forgetting that observed consequences shape imitation.

activity.prompt: Classify each consequence.

items.text: Headache goes away after taking rest, so you rest earlier next time
Nagging stops when you clean your room

quiz.q: In Pavlov's study, the bell after conditioning is the:
quiz.why: After conditioning, the bell alone triggers the response, so it is the conditioned stimulus (CS).
A variable-ratio schedule, where rewards come after an unpredictable number of responses, is the most resistant to extinction.

options: increases behaviour by removing something unpleasant
quiz.why: Negative reinforcement increases a behaviour by removing something unpleasant. It is not punishment.

quiz.q: Bobo doll studies are linked to:
quiz.why: The Bobo doll studies are by Albert Bandura, on observational learning.

quiz.q: Reappearance of a CR after extinction and rest:
quiz.why: The reappearance of a conditioned response after extinction and a rest is spontaneous recovery.

questions.q: Behaviourism focuses on:
questions.why: Behaviourism, as founded by Watson, focuses on observable behaviour rather than inner mental states.

questions.q: Lobe for vision:
questions.why: The occipital lobe, at the back of the brain, contains the visual cortex.

questions.q: Learning by watching others:
questions.why: Learning by watching others is observational learning, shown by Bandura.

questions.q: A study finds r = 0 between height and IQ. This means:
questions.why: r = 0 means no linear relationship between the variables, not a negative or perfect one.

questions.q: Area for language comprehension:
questions.why: Wernicke's area, in the temporal lobe, is the area for language comprehension. Broca's area is for speech production.

questions.q: Proximity principle:
options: nearby items seen as a group
questions.why: The Gestalt principle of proximity says that items near each other are seen as a group.

questions.q: Assertion: Experiments can establish cause and effect. Reason: They manipulate the IV and control other variables, often with random assignment.
questions.why: An experiment manipulates the IV and controls other variables, often with random assignment. This lets it show cause and effect, so both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Weber fraction for brightness 0.08; base 250 units. JND:
questions.why: By Weber's law, JND = k × base = 0.08 × 250 = 20 units.

questions.q: Gamblers persisting at slot machines illustrates:
questions.why: Gamblers persist at slot machines because payouts come after an unpredictable number of plays. That is variable-ratio reinforcement.

questions.q: Case: After a car accident, Ravi feels anxious at the sound of screeching brakes — and also at a squeaky door. The squeaky-door response shows:
questions.why: Feeling anxious at a similar sound, a squeaky door, after the original trigger shows stimulus generalisation: similar stimuli trigger the conditioned response.

questions.q: Damage to the hippocampus would most impair:
questions.why: The hippocampus is crucial for forming new long-term memories. Damage to it impairs this, not balance or vision.

questions.q: A researcher gives one group a sugar pill and tells them it is a memory drug; neither researcher nor participants know who got the real drug. This is a:
questions.why: A sugar pill for the control group (placebo) and no one knowing who got the real drug (double-blind) is a double-blind placebo-controlled design. It controls expectancy effects.

questions.q: Which pairing of neurotransmitter and function is correct?
questions.why: Acetylcholine is involved in muscle contraction and memory. GABA is mainly inhibitory, and dopamine has a role in reward.

questions.q: Taking an umbrella because you were drenched last time (avoiding rain) is maintained mainly by:
questions.why: Taking an umbrella to avoid getting wet is negative reinforcement: the behaviour is strengthened because it removes an unpleasant outcome.

questions.q: A test measures what it claims but gives different scores on repeated use. It is:
questions.why: A test can't be valid if it gives different scores on repeated use, since reliability is a precondition for validity. So this situation is impossible.
