Learners can describe Freud, the Big Five, Piaget and Erikson
Learners can recognise common disorders and know when and where to seek help

scenes.text: Tanvi reads a 6-digit OTP, looks away to answer a call, and forgets it.
Short-term memory is small and fragile unless we rehearse — the multi-store model explains why.

steps.title: Models
steps.body:
- **Atkinson–Shiffrin (1968)** multi-store: sensory memory → short-term memory (STM) → long-term memory (LTM); rehearsal transfers information
- STM capacity about **7 ± 2** items (Miller, 1956), duration ~ 18–30 s without rehearsal; **chunking** increases capacity
- **Working memory** (Baddeley & Hitch, 1974): central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad (episodic buffer added 2000)
- LTM: explicit (episodic, semantic) and implicit (procedural, priming)
- Levels of processing: deeper (meaning-based) processing → better recall

steps.title: Forgetting
steps.body:
- **Ebbinghaus forgetting curve**: rapid early loss, then levelling off
- Decay; **interference** — proactive (old blocks new) and retroactive (new blocks old)
- Retrieval failure (tip-of-the-tongue); encoding specificity (context cues)
- Memory is reconstructive (Loftus: wording of questions alters eyewitness reports)

steps.title: Solved: interference type
steps.body:
- After changing your phone PIN, you keep typing the old one → **proactive** interference
- After learning Spanish, your school French vocabulary fades → **retroactive** interference

steps.title: Solved: study plan
steps.body: Spaced practice beats cramming: review after 1 day, 3 days, 1 week, 1 month. Combine with retrieval practice (self-testing) and elaboration (link to examples). Each review flattens the forgetting curve.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping proactive and retroactive interference.
- Thinking memories are stored like video recordings.
- Treating STM and working memory as identical in every model.
- Believing re-reading is as effective as self-testing.

cards.back: New learning disrupts recall of old
Central executive, phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, episodic buffer

quiz.why: Miller (1956) found short-term memory holds about 7 ± 2 items.

quiz.q: Remembering how to ride a bicycle is:
quiz.why: Remembering how to ride a bicycle is procedural memory, the memory for skills and how to do things.
Hermann Ebbinghaus described the forgetting curve in 1885.
Grouping the digits into 98765-43210 is chunking. It reduces the number of units to remember.
Loftus's research on the misinformation effect showed that memory is reconstructive, not a perfect recording.

scenes.text: Ravi struggles with algebra but composes beautiful music; his sister tops maths but is shy in groups.
Are they both 'intelligent'? Theories disagree about what intelligence is.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body:
- **Spearman**: general factor **g** plus specific abilities (s)
- **Thurstone**: primary mental abilities
- **Cattell**: fluid (reasoning) vs crystallised (knowledge) intelligence
- **Gardner (1983)**: multiple intelligences — linguistic, logical-mathematical, spatial, musical, bodily-kinaesthetic, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic
- **Sternberg**: triarchic — analytical, creative, practical
- **Emotional intelligence** (Salovey & Mayer; popularised by Goleman)

steps.title: Measurement
steps.body:
- Binet–Simon scale (1905); **ratio IQ** = mental age/chronological age × 100 (Stern/Terman)
- Modern **deviation IQ**: mean 100, standard deviation 15; about 68% score 85–115, about 95% score 70–130
- Good tests are standardised, reliable and valid; watch for cultural bias
- Heredity and environment both matter (twin and adoption studies)

steps.title: Solved: ratio IQ
steps.body:
A child of 8 years performs like a typical 10-year-old.

- IQ = 10/8 × 100 = **125**
- A 12-year-old with mental age 9: IQ = 75

steps.title: Solved: deviation IQ
steps.body: IQ 130 is 2 SD above the mean ⇒ higher than about **97.5%** of the population (since 95% lie within ±2 SD, 2.5% lie above).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating IQ as fixed for life.
- Using ratio IQ for adults (mental age plateaus).
- Calling Gardner's intelligences 'learning styles'.
- Ignoring cultural fairness in test use.

activity.prompt: A child aged 10 has a mental age of 12. What is the ratio IQ?

quiz.q: The g factor was proposed by:
quiz.why: Charles Spearman proposed the general intelligence factor g in his two-factor theory.
On many deviation IQ scales, the standard deviation is 15 (mean 100).
Crystallised intelligence is accumulated knowledge and skills, in Cattell's theory. Fluid intelligence is abstract reasoning.
The triarchic theory, with analytical, creative and practical intelligence, is by Robert Sternberg.

quiz.q: About what % of people have IQ between 85 and 115?
quiz.why: IQ 85–115 is within one standard deviation of the mean (100 ± 15), which covers about 68% of people.

story.title: The quiet teen, the confident adult

scenes.text: Asha was a shy teenager unsure of who she was.
By her late twenties she had a clear sense of identity and close friendships — stages Erikson described.

steps.title: Personality
steps.body:
- **Freud**: id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle), superego (morality); **defence mechanisms** — repression, denial, projection, displacement, rationalisation, sublimation, regression
- **Trait approach**: **Big Five** (OCEAN) — openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism
- **Humanistic**: Rogers' self-concept and unconditional positive regard; Maslow's hierarchy (physiological → safety → belonging → esteem → self-actualisation)
- Assessment: self-report inventories; projective tests (Rorschach, TAT) — weaker reliability

steps.title: Development
steps.body:
**Piaget's cognitive stages**: sensorimotor (0–2, object permanence) → preoperational (2–7, egocentrism, no conservation) → concrete operational (7–11, conservation, logical with concrete things) → formal operational (11+, abstract reasoning).

**Erikson's psychosocial stages** (selected): trust vs mistrust (infancy); autonomy vs shame; initiative vs guilt; industry vs inferiority (school age); **identity vs role confusion** (adolescence); **intimacy vs isolation** (young adulthood); generativity vs stagnation; integrity vs despair (old age).

steps.title: Solved: name the defence
steps.body:
- Shouting at a younger sibling after being scolded by the boss → **displacement**
- Saying 'I didn't want that job anyway' after rejection → **rationalisation**
- Channelling anger into boxing → **sublimation**

steps.title: Solved: Piaget's conservation
steps.body: Pour equal water from a short wide glass into a tall thin one. A 5-year-old says the tall glass has more → **preoperational** (no conservation). A 9-year-old says it's the same → **concrete operational**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating Freud's theory as empirically established (it is influential but hard to test).
- Listing 'intelligence' as a Big Five trait.
- Mixing Piaget's (cognitive) and Erikson's (psychosocial) stages.
- Thinking stage ages are rigid.

activity.prompt: Match the example to the concept.
pairs: Blaming others for your own faults

quiz.why: The Big Five (OCEAN) are openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism.
Conservation, understanding that quantity stays the same despite changes in shape, appears in Piaget's concrete operational stage (about 7–11 years).
In Freud's theory, the ego works on the reality principle, balancing the id's demands and the real world. The id follows the pleasure principle.
Erikson's stage for young adults is intimacy vs isolation, about forming close relationships.
Self-actualisation is at the top of Maslow's hierarchy of needs.

scenes.text: For two months, Dev has lost interest in friends, sleeps badly and struggles to study. He tells himself it's 'just stress'.
A friend gently encourages him to talk to the college counsellor. Recognising signs early, and seeking help, matters.

steps.title: Understanding disorders
steps.body:
- Classification systems: **DSM-5-TR** (American Psychiatric Association) and **ICD-11** (WHO)
- Criteria often include distress, dysfunction in daily life, deviation from cultural norms, and duration
- **Biopsychosocial model**: genes and brain chemistry, thoughts and coping, relationships and environment interact
- Examples: anxiety disorders (generalised anxiety, panic, phobias), depressive disorders (persistent low mood, loss of interest, sleep/appetite change), OCD, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, PTSD
- Treatments: psychotherapy (e.g. CBT), medication prescribed by psychiatrists, social support — often combined

steps.title: When and where to seek help
steps.body:
Seek a professional (counsellor, clinical psychologist, psychiatrist, or doctor) when symptoms last more than about two weeks, affect study/work/relationships, or include thoughts of self-harm.

In India: **Tele-MANAS 14416** (free mental-health helpline), **112** for any emergency. If someone is in immediate danger, stay with them and call 112.

This is general education, not medical advice or diagnosis.

steps.title: Solved: myth or fact?
steps.body:
- 'Depression is just weakness' → **myth**: it is a health condition with biological and social causes
- 'Talking about suicide puts the idea in someone's head' → **myth**: asking directly and calmly can open the door to help
- 'Therapy can be effective without medication for many people' → **fact** (depends on the condition and severity)

steps.title: Solved: supportive response
steps.body:
A friend says, 'I can't cope anymore.'

- Listen without judging; reflect: 'That sounds really hard.'
- Ask about safety; encourage professional help; offer to sit with them while they call Tele-MANAS 14416
- Avoid: 'Just think positive' or promising secrecy if they are at risk

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Self-diagnosing from social media lists.
- Using clinical words casually ('I'm so OCD').
- Delaying help until a crisis.
- Believing medication alone or therapy alone is always the answer.

activity.prompt: Questions students often hesitate to ask

items.q: How do I know if it's stress or something more?
items.a: Stress usually eases when the pressure passes. If low mood, worry or sleep problems last more than two weeks or stop you functioning, talk to a counsellor or doctor.

items.q: Will seeing a counsellor go on my record?
items.a: Counselling is confidential, with limited exceptions such as serious risk of harm. Ask about confidentiality at the first session.

items.q: Is there free help in India?
items.a: Yes. Tele-MANAS 14416 is a free government mental-health helpline. Many colleges also have free counselling centres.

items.q: What if a friend tells me they want to die?
items.a: Take it seriously, stay with them, listen, and get help immediately — call 112 if they are in danger, or Tele-MANAS 14416.

quiz.why: ICD-11 is published by the World Health Organization (WHO). The APA publishes the DSM.

quiz.q: The biopsychosocial model says disorders arise from:
options: interacting biological, psychological and social factors
quiz.why: The biopsychosocial model says disorders arise from interacting biological, psychological and social factors, not from weak willpower or biology alone.
14416 is Tele-MANAS, India's free national tele-mental-health helpline. 1098 is Childline.
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) focuses on how thoughts, feelings and behaviours affect each other.

quiz.q: A helpful first response to a distressed friend:
options: listen without judging and encourage help
quiz.why: A good first response is to listen without judging and encourage them to seek help. Don't dismiss their feelings or promise to keep every secret, especially if their safety is at risk.

questions.q: STM holds information for about:
options: seconds to half a minute without rehearsal
questions.why: Without rehearsal, short-term memory holds information for only seconds to about half a minute.

questions.q: Multiple intelligences theory:
questions.why: Howard Gardner proposed multiple intelligences, in 1983.

questions.q: Piaget's first stage:
questions.why: Piaget's first stage is the sensorimotor stage, from birth to about 2 years.

questions.q: New phone number interferes with remembering your old one:
questions.why: A new phone number that interferes with remembering the old one is retroactive interference: new learning disrupts old memory.

questions.q: Ratio IQ: MA 6, CA 8:
questions.why: Ratio IQ = (mental age ÷ chronological age) × 100 = 6/8 × 100 = 75.

questions.q: Unconditional positive regard is central to:
questions.why: Unconditional positive regard is central to Carl Rogers's person-centred therapy.

questions.q: Assertion: Spaced practice improves retention. Reason: Repeated retrieval after delays strengthens memory traces and flattens the forgetting curve.
questions.why: Spaced practice improves retention, because repeated retrieval after delays strengthens memory traces and slows forgetting. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: IQ 115 on a deviation scale (mean 100, SD 15) is higher than roughly:
questions.why: IQ 115 is one SD above the mean (100, SD 15), which is about the 84th percentile. So it is higher than roughly 84% of people.

questions.q: A 4-year-old believes others see what she sees:
questions.why: A preoperational child who believes others see what she sees shows egocentrism, difficulty taking another's viewpoint.

questions.q: Case: After failing an exam, Neel says the paper was unfair though he hadn't studied. Defence mechanism:
questions.why: Blaming an 'unfair' paper after not studying is rationalisation: giving a plausible excuse instead of the real reason.

questions.q: In Baddeley's model, rehearsing a phone number silently uses the:
questions.why: Silently rehearsing a phone number uses the phonological loop in Baddeley's working memory model, which handles verbal information.

questions.q: Which response to a friend expressing hopelessness is MOST appropriate?
options: Listen, ask about safety, and help them contact a professional or Tele-MANAS 14416
Tell them everyone feels that way
questions.why: Listen, ask about safety, and help them reach a professional or Tele-MANAS (14416). Telling them everyone feels that way, avoiding them or posting online does not help.

questions.q: Fluid intelligence tends to:
options: peak in early adulthood and decline slowly
questions.why: Fluid intelligence tends to peak in early adulthood and decline slowly. Crystallised intelligence can keep growing.

questions.q: A projective test's main weakness:
options: lower reliability and validity of scoring
questions.why: Projective tests, like inkblots, have lower reliability and validity because scoring depends on subjective interpretation.

questions.q: Erikson's 'generativity vs stagnation' concerns:
options: reflecting on life in old age
contributing to the next generation in middle adulthood
questions.why: Generativity vs stagnation, in middle adulthood, is about contributing to the next generation through work, family and community.

courses.title: Political Science I · state, liberty, justice, democracy, power
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: The state and social contract theories, liberty, equality and Rawlsian justice, models of democracy, and power, authority, legitimacy and sovereignty.
outcomes: Learners can compare Hobbes, Locke and Rousseau
Learners can distinguish negative and positive liberty and explain Rawls
Learners can compare elitist, pluralist and deliberative democracy
Learners can apply Weber's types of authority

lessons.title: The state and social contract theories

scenes.text: A shipwrecked group on an island must decide: who decides disputes, and why should anyone obey?
Social contract thinkers asked the same question about real societies.

steps.title: The state
steps.body:
Elements: **population, territory, government, sovereignty** (some add international recognition).

**Social contract theories**:
- **Thomas Hobbes** (*Leviathan*, 1651): state of nature is 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'; people surrender rights to an absolute sovereign for security
- **John Locke** (*Two Treatises of Government*, 1689): natural rights to life, liberty and property; limited government by consent; right to resist tyranny
- **Jean-Jacques Rousseau** (*The Social Contract*, 1762): sovereignty lies with the people's **general will**; 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains'

steps.title: Solved: who said it?
steps.body:
- Government exists to protect property, and can be overthrown if it violates rights → **Locke**
- Without a strong sovereign, life is war of all against all → **Hobbes**
- Laws are legitimate only if they express the general will → **Rousseau**

steps.title: Solved: apply to India
steps.body: The Preamble begins 'We, the people of India' — sovereignty flows from the people (a Lockean/Rousseauian idea), while fundamental rights limit state power (Lockean).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating government and state as the same (governments change; the state continues).
- Mixing up Hobbes's absolutism with Locke's limited government.
- Reading the social contract as a real historical event (it is a thought experiment).

activity.prompt: Match the thinker to the idea.
pairs: Man is by nature a political animal

quiz.why: Leviathan (1651) was written by Thomas Hobbes.
Sovereignty, supreme authority, is an essential element of a state, along with population, territory and government.
Locke's natural rights are life, liberty and property.
The 'general will' is associated with Rousseau, in The Social Contract (1762).

quiz.q: Social contract theories are best seen as:
quiz.why: Social contract theories are best seen as thought experiments about the legitimacy of political authority, not as historical records.

scenes.text: Imagine designing society's rules without knowing whether you'll be born rich or poor, abled or disabled.
John Rawls argued you'd choose fair rules — that is the veil of ignorance.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Liberty**: Isaiah Berlin ('Two Concepts of Liberty', 1958) — **negative liberty** (freedom from interference) vs **positive liberty** (freedom to be self-governing/realise potential)
- J. S. Mill (*On Liberty*, 1859): **harm principle** — power may be exercised over anyone only to prevent harm to others
- **Equality**: formal (equal before law), of opportunity, of outcome; affirmative action/reservations as substantive equality
- **Justice**: **John Rawls** (*A Theory of Justice*, 1971): original position and **veil of ignorance**; principles — equal basic liberties; inequalities allowed only with fair equality of opportunity and to benefit the least advantaged (**difference principle**)
- Critics: Robert Nozick (entitlement theory, minimal state); communitarians; Amartya Sen's comparative, capability-focused approach

steps.title: Solved: negative or positive?
steps.body:
- A law banning censorship of books → expands **negative liberty**
- Free schooling so children can choose their life paths → expands **positive liberty**

steps.title: Solved: Rawls applied
steps.body: Higher pay for doctors is acceptable under the difference principle **if** it attracts talent that improves health for the least advantaged and posts are open to all. It is unjust if the inequality brings them no benefit.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Rawls demands perfect equality (he permits some inequalities).
- Using Mill's harm principle to justify paternalism (he rejected harm-to-self as grounds).
- Confusing equality of opportunity with equality of outcome.

activity.prompt: Negative or positive liberty?

items.text: No police permission needed to hold a peaceful meeting
Skill programmes enabling people to pursue careers

quiz.why: 'Two Concepts of Liberty' (1958) is by Isaiah Berlin.
The veil of ignorance, in the original position, is John Rawls's idea.
The harm principle is from John Stuart Mill's On Liberty. Liberty may be restricted only to prevent harm to others.
Rawls's difference principle allows inequalities only if they benefit the least advantaged.
Robert Nozick argued for a minimal state and an entitlement theory, in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974).

scenes.text: A city council decision on a flyover seems to follow the wishes of a few big builders.
Elitists say a few always rule; pluralists say many groups compete; deliberative democrats say reasoned public debate should decide.

steps.title: Models
steps.body:
- **Direct democracy** (ancient Athens; referendums) vs **representative democracy**
- **Liberal democracy**: elections plus rights, rule of law, independent courts
- **Elite theory**: Pareto, Mosca, Michels ('iron law of oligarchy') — power concentrated in a minority; C. Wright Mills' 'power elite'
- **Pluralism**: Robert Dahl — power dispersed among competing groups; polyarchy
- **Deliberative democracy**: legitimacy from reasoned public discussion (Habermas)
- **Participatory democracy**: active citizen involvement (e.g. gram sabhas)

steps.title: Solved: classify the claim
steps.body:
- 'Every organisation, even a socialist party, ends up run by a few leaders' → **Michels / elite theory**
- 'Farmers' unions, industry bodies and NGOs bargain; no single group dominates' → **pluralism**
- 'Citizens' assemblies weigh evidence before deciding' → **deliberative democracy**

steps.title: Solved: India's institutions
steps.body: Universal adult franchise since the first general elections (1951–52), an independent Election Commission, and constitutionally mandated gram sabhas (73rd Amendment, 1992) combine representative and participatory elements.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating democracy only with elections.
- Thinking pluralism means all groups have equal power.
- Calling India a direct democracy.

activity.prompt: Match the thinker to the theory.

quiz.why: Robert Michels developed the 'iron law of oligarchy' in 1911: organisations tend to be ruled by a few.
Polyarchy is associated with Robert Dahl, a pluralist theorist.
Referendums, where citizens vote directly on an issue, are a feature of direct democracy.

options: rights and rule of law plus elections
quiz.why: Liberal democracy combines elections with rights and the rule of law, which limit those in power.
Gram sabhas, village assemblies, show participatory democracy, since citizens take part directly.

scenes.text: Drivers stop at a red light at 2 a.m. with no police around.
They obey because they accept the rule as legitimate — authority, not mere force.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Power**: ability to make others act as one wishes (Weber); faces of power — decision-making, agenda-setting (Bachrach & Baratz), shaping preferences (Lukes, 1974)
- **Authority** = legitimate power. **Max Weber's three types**: **traditional** (custom, monarchy), **charismatic** (exceptional personal qualities), **legal-rational** (rules and offices, bureaucracy)
- **Legitimacy**: belief that rule is rightful
- **Sovereignty**: Jean Bodin; John Austin's monistic view (command of a determinate sovereign); **pluralist** critique (Harold Laski) — power shared with associations; popular sovereignty; external sovereignty in international law

steps.title: Solved: Weber's types
steps.body:
- A village elder obeyed because 'it has always been so' → **traditional**
- A freedom-movement leader followed for personal magnetism → **charismatic**
- A district collector obeyed because of the office and law → **legal-rational**

steps.title: Solved: three faces of power
steps.body: A city never discusses slum housing because powerful groups keep it off the council agenda → **second face** (agenda-setting). Residents themselves believe nothing can change → **third face** (shaping preferences).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using power and authority as synonyms.
- Thinking charismatic authority is stable over generations (it tends to be 'routinised').
- Treating Austin's monistic sovereignty as the only view.

activity.prompt: Which type of authority (Weber)?

items.text: Elected Prime Minister acting under the Constitution

quiz.q: Weber's types of authority do NOT include:
quiz.why: Weber's three types of authority are traditional, charismatic and legal-rational. 'Coercive-divine' is not one of them.
Bureaucracy, with rules and offices, is linked to Weber's legal-rational authority.
Steven Lukes wrote about the 'three dimensions of power' (1974).
Harold Laski gave a pluralist critique of sovereignty, arguing that authority is shared among groups.
Legitimacy is the belief that the rule or ruler is rightful. It is more than force, wealth or size.

questions.q: The four elements of a state include:
questions.why: The four elements of a state are population, territory, government and sovereignty. A capital city, religion or king isn't essential.

questions.q: A Theory of Justice (1971):
questions.why: A Theory of Justice (1971) is by John Rawls.

questions.q: Legitimate power is called:
questions.why: Legitimate power is called authority, as in Weber. Coercion and violence lack legitimacy.

questions.q: Locke supported:
questions.why: Locke supported limited government based on the consent of the governed.

questions.q: Positive liberty concerns:
questions.why: In Berlin's account, positive liberty is about the capacity for self-mastery. Negative liberty is the absence of interference.

questions.q: Elite theorists include:
questions.why: Pareto and Mosca are classical elite theorists. Dahl and Lindblom are pluralists.

questions.q: Assertion: Hobbes favoured an absolute sovereign. Reason: He saw the state of nature as a war of all against all.
questions.why: Hobbes saw the state of nature as a war of all against all, so he favoured an absolute sovereign to provide security. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Mill's harm principle justifies restricting liberty to prevent:
options: economic loss to the state only
questions.why: Mill's harm principle says liberty can be restricted only to prevent harm to others. Offence or harm to oneself is not enough.

questions.q: Charismatic authority tends over time to become:
options: routinised into traditional or legal forms
questions.why: Charismatic authority depends on one person, so over time it tends to be routinised into traditional or legal-rational forms.

questions.q: Case: An NGO, a trade union and a business lobby each win some and lose some policy battles. Best fits:
questions.why: When several groups win some policy battles and lose others, influence is dispersed. This best fits pluralism.

questions.q: Behind the veil of ignorance, Rawls argues people would choose:
options: equal basic liberties and the difference principle
questions.why: Rawls argues that, behind the veil of ignorance, people would choose equal basic liberties and the difference principle, using maximin reasoning.

questions.q: Keeping an issue off the agenda reflects which face of power?
questions.why: Keeping an issue off the agenda is the second face of power (non-decision-making), described by Bachrach and Baratz.

questions.q: Which statement about Rousseau is accurate?
options: Sovereignty of the general will cannot be represented
questions.why: Rousseau held that sovereignty lies in the general will and cannot be represented. Leviathan is Hobbes's work.

questions.q: Nozick's critique of Rawls rests on:
options: entitlement and historical justice of holdings
questions.why: Nozick's critique of Rawls rests on entitlement and the historical justice of holdings, not on a patterned end-state of distribution.

questions.q: Austin's theory of sovereignty is described as:
questions.why: Austin's theory of sovereignty is monistic: it places sovereignty in a single, determinate, supreme authority.

courses.title: Political Science II · Indian Constitution and government
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Making of the Constitution and the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Duties, the Union executive and Parliament, and federalism, judiciary and local government. General education, not legal advice.
outcomes: Learners can explain how the Constitution was made and what the Preamble says
Learners can distinguish rights, directive principles and duties and name the writs
Learners can describe the President, Prime Minister and law-making in Parliament
Learners can explain federal lists, Article 356, judicial review and panchayati raj

lessons.title: Making of the Constitution and the Preamble

scenes.text: Every 26 November, schools mark Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas).
On that day in 1949 the Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution; it came into force on 26 January 1950.

steps.title: Key facts
steps.body:
- Constituent Assembly first met on **9 December 1946**; Dr Rajendra Prasad became its permanent President
- **Dr B. R. Ambedkar** chaired the Drafting Committee
- Adopted **26 November 1949**; came into force **26 January 1950**
- Borrowed features: parliamentary system (UK), fundamental rights and judicial review (USA), directive principles (Ireland), federation with a strong centre (Canada), emergency provisions (Germany's Weimar constitution)

steps.title: The Preamble
steps.body:
Declares India a **sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic** and secures **justice** (social, economic, political), **liberty** (of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship), **equality** (of status and opportunity) and **fraternity** (assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the nation).

The words 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' were added by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**. In *Kesavananda Bharati* (1973) the Supreme Court held the Preamble is part of the Constitution.

steps.title: Solved: date check
steps.body: - Why 26 January? It recalls **Purna Swaraj** day (26 January 1930), after the Lahore session of the Congress (December 1929) resolved for complete independence.

steps.title: Solved: Preamble values in practice
steps.body:
- Reservations in education and jobs → **equality of opportunity** and **social justice**
- Freedom to practise any religion → **liberty of belief, faith and worship** and **secularism**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the Constitution came into force on 26 November 1949.
- Thinking 'socialist' and 'secular' were in the original 1950 Preamble.
- Calling Ambedkar President of the Constituent Assembly (he chaired the Drafting Committee).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Order these constitutional milestones.

events.text: Purna Swaraj day observed on 26 January

quiz.why: B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly.

quiz.q: The Constitution came into force on:
quiz.why: The Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950, celebrated as Republic Day. It was adopted on 26 November 1949.
The word 'secular' was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

quiz.q: Directive principles were inspired by the constitution of:
quiz.why: The Directive Principles of State Policy were inspired by the Constitution of Ireland.

quiz.q: Preamble is part of the Constitution per:
quiz.why: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution.

lessons.title: Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Duties

scenes.text: In 1977, Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded without giving her a hearing.
In 1978 the Supreme Court held that any law depriving personal liberty must be 'just, fair and reasonable' — expanding Article 21.

steps.title: Part III and Part IV
steps.body:
**Fundamental Rights (Part III, Arts 12–35)**: equality (14–18; Art 17 abolishes untouchability), freedoms (19–22; Art 21 life and personal liberty; Art 21A education 6–14 years), against exploitation (23–24), religion (25–28), cultural and educational (29–30), **constitutional remedies (Art 32)** — Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. Right to property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now a legal right (Art 300A).

**Writs**: habeas corpus (produce the detained person), mandamus (command a public duty), prohibition (stop a lower court), certiorari (quash an order), quo warranto (by what authority).

**Directive Principles (Part IV, Arts 36–51)**: non-justiciable guidelines for policy (e.g. Art 39, 44 uniform civil code, 45 early childhood care, 48A environment).

**Fundamental Duties (Part IVA, Art 51A)**: added by the 42nd Amendment (1976); now **11** duties (the 11th added by the 86th Amendment, 2002).

steps.title: Solved: which writ?
steps.body:
- Police detain a student without producing him before a magistrate → **habeas corpus**
- A municipal body refuses to perform a statutory duty → **mandamus**
- A person holds a public office without legal qualification → **quo warranto**

steps.title: Solved: rights vs principles
steps.body:
- Free and compulsory education for 6–14-year-olds is a **fundamental right** (Art 21A, 86th Amendment, 2002)
- Early childhood care up to six years is a **directive principle** (Art 45)
- Protecting the environment is both a directive (Art 48A) and a duty (Art 51A(g))

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying DPSPs are enforceable in court (they are not, though courts use them to interpret rights).
- Listing the right to property as a fundamental right.
- Confusing Art 32 (Supreme Court) with Art 226 (High Courts, wider scope).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Match the writ to its purpose.
pairs: Command performance of a public duty
Stop a lower court exceeding jurisdiction
Question authority to hold public office

quiz.why: Article 32 gives the right to constitutional remedies: the right to approach the Supreme Court to enforce fundamental rights through writs.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
The Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA of the Constitution (Article 51A).
Article 21A gives the right to education for children aged 6–14, added by the 86th Amendment.
In Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Supreme Court expanded Article 21: the procedure for restricting life and liberty must be fair, just and reasonable.

lessons.title: The Union: President, Prime Minister and Parliament

scenes.text: A bill on data protection is introduced in the Lok Sabha, debated, sent to a committee, passed by both Houses.
Only after the President's assent does it become an Act.

steps.title: Executive
steps.body:
- **President** (Art 52) — head of state; elected indirectly by an electoral college of elected MPs and elected MLAs of states (and Delhi and Puducherry) (Art 54); acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Art 74)
- **Prime Minister** heads the Council of Ministers, which is collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha** (Art 75)
- Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha

steps.title: Parliament
steps.body:
- **Lok Sabha**: 543 elected seats at present; term 5 years unless dissolved
- **Rajya Sabha**: maximum 250 (up to 238 elected by state/UT legislators + 12 nominated); permanent body, one-third retire every 2 years
- **Money bill** (Art 110): introduced only in Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days; Speaker certifies
- Ordinary bill deadlock → **joint sitting** (Art 108), presided by the Speaker
- Constitutional amendment (Art 368): special majority, some also needing ratification by half the states; no joint sitting
- **106th Amendment (2023)** provides one-third reservation for women in the Lok Sabha and state assemblies, to take effect after delimitation following the next census

steps.title: Solved: which procedure?
steps.body:
- Lok Sabha passes a tax bill; Rajya Sabha suggests changes after 10 days → Lok Sabha may accept or reject; the bill is deemed passed (**money bill**)
- Houses disagree on an ordinary bill for over six months → President may summon a **joint sitting**

steps.title: Solved: confidence
steps.body: If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, the **Council of Ministers must resign** (collective responsibility). The Rajya Sabha cannot remove the government.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the President is directly elected.
- Allowing joint sittings for constitutional amendments or money bills.
- Thinking the Rajya Sabha can be dissolved.
- Saying the women's reservation already applies to the 2024 Lok Sabha (it applies after delimitation).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Order the stages of an ordinary bill.
items: Second reading (general discussion, committee scrutiny, clause-by-clause)
Third reading and passage in the first House
Same stages in the other House
President's assent — the bill becomes an Act

quiz.q: Money bills are defined in Article:
quiz.why: Money bills are defined in Article 110.

quiz.q: Joint sitting is presided over by the:
quiz.why: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting of the two Houses (Article 118(4)).

quiz.q: Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to:
quiz.why: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)).
The maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha is 250 (Article 80): 238 elected members and up to 12 nominated.

quiz.q: Rajya Sabha can hold a money bill for at most:
quiz.why: The Rajya Sabha can hold a money bill for at most 14 days (Article 109). Then it is deemed passed.

scenes.text: Police and public order are state subjects; defence and railways are Union subjects; education is on the concurrent list.
Indian federalism divides powers — and courts police the boundaries.

steps.title: Federal features
steps.body:
- **Seventh Schedule**: Union List, State List, Concurrent List (residuary powers with the Union)
- Strong centre: single citizenship, all-India services, emergency powers, governors appointed by the President
- **Article 356** (President's rule): limited by *S. R. Bommai v Union of India* (1994) — floor test, judicial review
- Cooperative federalism: GST Council (Art 279A), Finance Commission (Art 280), Inter-State Council (Art 263)

steps.title: Judiciary and local government
steps.body:
- **Supreme Court** (Art 124); High Courts (Art 214); integrated judiciary
- **Judicial review** and the **basic structure doctrine** (*Kesavananda Bharati*, 1973): Parliament can amend but not destroy basic features
- Public interest litigation widened access to justice from the late 1970s–80s
- **73rd and 74th Amendments (1992)**: constitutional status for panchayats and municipalities; three-tier panchayati raj (village, block, district), five-year terms, State Election Commissions, at least **one-third reservation for women** (many states provide 50%)

steps.title: Solved: which list?
steps.body:
- Defence, foreign affairs, banking → **Union List**
- Police, public health, agriculture → **State List**
- Education, forests, marriage and divorce → **Concurrent List** (education and forests moved there by the 42nd Amendment)

steps.title: Solved: basic structure
steps.body: An amendment to remove judicial review entirely would likely be struck down because judicial review is part of the basic structure (as affirmed in later cases like *Minerva Mills*, 1980).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing residuary powers with the states (they are with the Union in India).
- Saying Art 356 is beyond judicial review after Bommai.
- Thinking panchayats existed constitutionally before 1992 (they existed under state laws but gained constitutional status in 1992).

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Which list in the Seventh Schedule?

quiz.q: Residuary powers in India lie with:
quiz.why: Residuary powers, for subjects not listed anywhere, lie with the Union (Article 248).
S. R. Bommai (1994) concerned Article 356 (President's rule). It limited its misuse.

quiz.q: Panchayati raj got constitutional status by the:
quiz.why: Panchayati raj got constitutional status by the 73rd Amendment (1992). The 74th covers municipalities.

quiz.q: Basic structure doctrine was laid down in:
quiz.why: The basic structure doctrine was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) by a 13-judge bench.
The GST Council is under Article 279A, added by the 101st Amendment.

questions.q: India's Constitution was adopted on:
questions.why: The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 (Constitution Day) and came into force on 26 January 1950.

questions.q: Fundamental Rights are in Part:
questions.why: Fundamental Rights are in Part III of the Constitution (Articles 12–35).

questions.q: Head of the Union executive (formally):
questions.why: The President is the formal head of the Union executive (Article 53).

questions.q: Writ to release an unlawfully detained person:
questions.why: Habeas corpus ('have the body') is the writ to release a person who is unlawfully detained.

questions.q: Money bills can be introduced in:
questions.why: Money bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha (Article 109).

questions.q: Education is on the:
questions.why: Education has been on the Concurrent List since 1976, so both Union and states can legislate on it.

questions.q: Assertion: DPSPs are not enforceable by courts. Reason: Article 37 declares them non-justiciable though fundamental in governance.
questions.why: DPSPs are non-justiciable, since Article 37 says courts can't enforce them, yet they are fundamental in governance. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Number of Fundamental Duties today:
questions.why: There are 11 Fundamental Duties today. The 11th, a duty to provide education opportunities, was added in 2002.

questions.q: The President is elected by:
questions.why: The President is elected by an electoral college of elected MPs and elected MLAs.

questions.q: Case: The Rajya Sabha rejects an ordinary bill passed by the Lok Sabha. Constitutional route to resolve:
questions.why: A deadlock between the Houses on an ordinary bill is resolved by a joint sitting under Article 108.

questions.q: Which can NOT be done at a joint sitting?
options: resolve a deadlock on an ordinary bill
questions.why: A joint sitting cannot be used to pass a constitutional amendment. Article 368 needs each House to pass it separately.

questions.q: Right to property today is a:
questions.why: Right to property is no longer a fundamental right. After the 44th Amendment it is a legal (constitutional) right under Article 300A.

questions.q: Bommai (1994) held that the majority of a state government should be tested:
options: on the floor of the House
questions.why: Bommai (1994) held that a state government's majority must be tested on the floor of the House (a floor test), not by the Governor's opinion alone.

questions.q: The women's reservation under the 106th Amendment applies to:
options: Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies after delimitation
questions.why: The 106th Amendment reserves seats for women in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies, and it will take effect after delimitation.

questions.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
questions.why: Article 21A is the right to education. Article 110 is money bills, Art 17 is untouchability and Art 356 is President's rule.

courses.title: BA Psychology & Political Science · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: One-page sheets for Psychology and Political Science, a solved practice set of case questions and a 20-question mock exam.
outcomes: Learners can recall key theorists, terms and articles
Learners can apply concepts to short cases
Learners can structure 10-mark answers

scenes.text: Sneha revises each theory as a triplet: name, core idea, everyday example.
Examples are what turn a 6/10 answer into a 9/10.

steps.title: Psychology essentials
steps.body:
- Wundt 1879; Freud; Watson/Skinner; Maslow/Rogers; cognitive
- IV/DV; correlation ≠ causation; reliability vs validity; ethics
- Broca (production), Wernicke (comprehension), hippocampus (memory), amygdala (fear)
- Weber ΔI/I = k; Gestalt: closure, proximity, similarity, figure–ground
- Pavlov UCS/UCR/CS/CR; Skinner reinforcement/punishment; VR schedule; Bandura
- STM 7 ± 2; working memory; proactive vs retroactive interference
- IQ = MA/CA × 100; deviation IQ mean 100, SD 15
- Big Five; Piaget 4 stages; Erikson 8 stages
- DSM-5-TR, ICD-11; help: Tele-MANAS 14416, emergency 112

steps.title: Answer frame
steps.body: Define → explain theory with key terms → evaluate (evidence and criticism) → apply to an example.

steps.title: Common slips
steps.body:
- Swapping Broca's (production) and Wernicke's (comprehension)
- Calling negative reinforcement punishment
- Mixing proactive and retroactive interference
- Treating correlation as causation
- Self-diagnosing mental-health conditions — for real concerns see a professional (Tele-MANAS 14416)

cards.back: Removing something unpleasant to increase a behaviour
Grouping items to expand STM capacity

quiz.q: Conditioned fear in 'Little Albert' was studied by:
quiz.why: The 'Little Albert' experiment on conditioned fear was by Watson and Rayner (1920).
Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter. GABA is inhibitory.
Retroactive interference is when new learning disrupts memory of older information. Proactive is the reverse.

quiz.q: Industry vs inferiority is Erikson's stage for:
quiz.why: Industry vs inferiority is Erikson's stage for school age, roughly 6–12 years.

scenes.text: Ravi pairs each article number with a one-line meaning and each thinker with a book and year.
Precise references impress examiners.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body:
- Hobbes *Leviathan* 1651; Locke 1689; Rousseau 1762
- Mill harm principle 1859; Berlin liberty 1958; Rawls 1971; Nozick 1974
- Elite: Pareto, Mosca, Michels; pluralism: Dahl; deliberative: Habermas
- Weber: traditional, charismatic, legal-rational authority; Lukes three faces of power

steps.title: Indian Constitution
steps.body:
- CA met 9 Dec 1946; adopted 26 Nov 1949; in force 26 Jan 1950
- Preamble; 42nd Amendment 1976 added socialist, secular, integrity; Fundamental Duties
- Part III (12–35): 14, 17, 19, 21, 21A, 32; writs (5)
- Part IV (36–51) non-justiciable; Part IVA (51A) 11 duties
- Art 52, 54, 74, 75; Art 108 joint sitting; Art 110 money bill; Art 368 amendment
- Seventh Schedule; Art 356 and Bommai 1994; Kesavananda 1973 basic structure
- 73rd/74th Amendments 1992; 106th Amendment 2023 (women's reservation after delimitation)

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Match the article to its subject.

quiz.why: Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
Isaiah Berlin's two concepts of liberty are negative and positive liberty (1958).
The basic structure doctrine comes from Kesavananda Bharati, decided in 1973.
Legal-rational authority rests on rules and law, as with a civil servant acting under law. A hereditary chief is traditional, and a cult leader is charismatic.
Under Article 80, the Rajya Sabha has up to 12 members nominated by the President, for their special knowledge in areas like art, science, literature and social service.

lessons.title: Mock paper A — solved case questions

scenes.text: 20 minutes: read each case and name the concept before answering.
Compare with the model answers.

steps.title: Solved: psychology case
steps.body:
A student studies late into the night only when the exam is a week away and slacks off after it — like workers paid every Friday who work harder near payday.

- Pattern matches a **fixed-interval schedule** (scalloped response near the reinforcement time)

steps.title: Solved: political theory case
steps.body:
A government argues it must ban junk food 'for people's own good'.

- Mill would object — harm to self is not grounds for coercion; persuasion or information is preferable. A positive-liberty view might support it as enabling healthier choices.

steps.title: Solved: constitution case
steps.body:
A state government is dismissed without a floor test based only on the Governor's report.

- Under *Bommai* (1994), the proper test of majority is the **floor of the House**; the proclamation is subject to judicial review.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal or medical advice.

activity.prompt: Can you write a 10-mark answer on:
items: Classical vs operant conditioning with examples

quiz.why: A pay cheque every Friday is a reward after a fixed time period, so it is a fixed-interval schedule.

options: he opposed coercion for one's own good
quiz.why: Mill opposed using coercion for a person's own good. His harm principle limits interference to preventing harm to others.
Bommai's key test is the floor test: a government's majority must be decided in the legislature, not by the Governor's view alone.
The idea of a 'power elite' controlling key decisions is C. Wright Mills's. Dahl's pluralism says power is dispersed.

quiz.q: A child insisting the moon follows her is showing:
quiz.why: A child who insists the moon follows her cannot see things from another's view and mixes her own view with reality. That is egocentrism, in the preoperational stage.

questions.q: Psychology is the scientific study of:
questions.why: Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. It isn't limited to animals, the brain or dreams.

questions.q: Lok Sabha's normal term:
questions.why: The Lok Sabha's normal term is 5 years from its first sitting (Article 83), unless dissolved earlier.

questions.q: Classical conditioning was discovered by:
questions.why: Ivan Pavlov discovered classical conditioning, in his experiments with dogs.

questions.q: General will:
questions.why: The 'general will' is Rousseau's idea, from The Social Contract (1762).

questions.q: Writ commanding a public official to perform a duty:
questions.why: Mandamus ('we command') is the writ that orders a public official to perform a public duty.

questions.q: Object permanence develops in the:
questions.why: Object permanence, knowing that objects continue to exist when out of sight, develops in the sensorimotor stage, in infancy.

questions.q: Negative liberty means:
questions.why: Negative liberty means freedom from interference by others. Positive liberty is the capacity for self-mastery.

questions.q: Amygdala is most linked to:
questions.why: The amygdala is most linked to emotion, especially fear.

questions.q: Assertion: The Rajya Sabha cannot remove the Council of Ministers. Reason: Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
questions.why: Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)). So the Rajya Sabha can't remove the Council of Ministers. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Weber fraction 0.05; weight 800 g. JND:
questions.why: By Weber's law, JND = fraction × base = 0.05 × 800 g = 40 g.

questions.q: Which amendment added Fundamental Duties?
questions.why: The Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

questions.q: Deviation IQ 85 is how many SD from the mean?
questions.why: z = (85 − 100)/15 = −1, so a deviation IQ of 85 is one standard deviation below the mean.

questions.q: Case: A teacher gives stickers at random intervals for good behaviour. Schedule:
questions.why: Stickers at random time intervals follow a variable-interval schedule: the timing is unpredictable and depends on time, not the number of responses.

questions.q: Case: A citizen's PIL asks the Supreme Court to direct a state to stop illegal mining. Likely writ:
questions.why: A PIL asking the court to direct a state to carry out its duty (stop illegal mining) fits the writ of mandamus, which enforces a public or statutory duty.

questions.q: Rawls's difference principle would favour a tax policy that:
options: maximises the position of the worst-off
questions.why: Rawls's difference principle says inequalities are fair only if they benefit the least advantaged. So it favours a tax policy that maximises the position of the worst-off (maximin).

questions.q: Michels' iron law states organisations tend toward:
questions.why: Michels' iron law of oligarchy says that organisations, even democratic ones, tend towards rule by a few leaders.

questions.q: A patient can't form new explicit memories but learns a new motor skill. This suggests:
options: separate systems for explicit and procedural memory
questions.why: A patient who can't form new explicit memories but still learns a motor skill shows that the two use separate memory systems. This dissociation was seen in patient H.M.

questions.q: Which statement about Article 368 is correct?
options: Amendments can be passed at a joint sitting
Some amendments also need ratification by half the state legislatures
questions.why: Under Article 368, some amendments, such as those on federal provisions, also need ratification by at least half of the state legislatures. A joint sitting cannot pass an amendment, and the basic structure can't be destroyed.

questions.q: Lukes's third face of power refers to:
questions.why: Lukes's third face of power is the shaping of people's preferences and perceptions, so they accept the existing order without open conflict.

questions.q: A study shows ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. The best explanation:
questions.why: Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer because of a third variable, hot weather. This shows that correlation doesn't prove causation.

uni-ba-humanities-b.description: Core BA papers in History (ancient, medieval and modern India) and Sociology (classical thinkers and Indian society), with source-based reasoning, timelines, case questions and unit exams.

courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: The Harappan civilisation, the Vedic age, Mahajanapadas with Buddhism and Jainism, the Mauryan and Gupta empires, and the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara, the Mughals and Bhakti–Sufi traditions.
outcomes: Learners can describe Harappan town planning, economy and sources
Learners can explain the rise of Magadha and the teachings of Buddha and Mahavira
Learners can analyse Ashoka's dhamma and Gupta achievements using sources
Learners can explain key institutions of the Sultanate and Mughal states

scenes.text: In the 1920s, archaeologists dug at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro and found grid-like streets, baked-brick houses and covered drains.
With no deciphered script, historians read this civilisation through its bricks, seals, beads and weights.

steps.title: Key features
steps.body:
- Excavations: Harappa (Daya Ram Sahni, 1921), Mohenjo-daro (R. D. Banerji, 1922)
- Mature phase about **2600–1900 BCE**
- Planned cities: citadel and lower town, grid streets, **standardised bricks (ratio about 1 : 2 : 4)**, covered drains; the **Great Bath** at Mohenjo-daro
- Sites: **Lothal** (Gujarat; dockyard and bead-making), **Kalibangan** (Rajasthan; ploughed field), **Dholavira** (Gujarat; water reservoirs; UNESCO World Heritage Site, 2021), Rakhigarhi (Haryana)
- Economy: agriculture (wheat, barley), crafts (beads, shell, metal), long-distance trade (including with Mesopotamia), standardised weights
- Seals (mostly steatite) with an **undeciphered script**
- Decline (c. 1900 BCE onwards): likely multiple causes — climate change, shifting rivers, decline of trade; the 'Aryan invasion' explanation is no longer accepted as the cause

steps.title: Solved: reading evidence
steps.body:
Finding: identical weights at sites hundreds of kilometres apart.

- Inference: a shared system of **standardised measurement**, suggesting coordinated trade and possibly some central authority
- Caution: we cannot name rulers — there are no deciphered texts

steps.title: Solved: match site to feature
steps.body:
- Dockyard → **Lothal**
- Great Bath → **Mohenjo-daro**
- Ploughed field → **Kalibangan**
- Elaborate water management → **Dholavira**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming the script has been deciphered.
- Presenting a single cause for the decline as certain.
- Mixing Harappan and Vedic features (e.g. horses and iron are not typical Harappan finds).
- Treating all sites as identical — regional variation existed.

activity.prompt: Match the Harappan site to its notable find.

quiz.why: The Harappan script is still undeciphered. Brahmi and Kharosthi are later scripts.
Lothal, in Gujarat, has a famous dockyard, evidence of Harappan maritime trade.
The mature Harappan phase dates to about 2600–1900 BCE, in the Bronze Age.
Harappan bricks have a standard ratio of about 1 : 2 : 4 for thickness, width and length.

quiz.q: Dholavira was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in:
quiz.why: Dholavira was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

lessons.title: Vedic age, Mahajanapadas, Buddhism and Jainism

story.title: The prince who left the palace

scenes.text: A prince of the Shakya clan left home in search of an answer to suffering.
Enlightened at Bodh Gaya, he gave his first sermon at Sarnath. Buddhism spread across Asia.

steps.title: From Vedas to kingdoms
steps.body:
- **Rig Veda** (earliest text; composed roughly 1500–1000 BCE): pastoral life, tribal assemblies (sabha, samiti)
- **Later Vedic** period (c. 1000–600 BCE): iron, agriculture expands into the Ganga valley, varna hierarchy sharpens
- **Sixteen Mahajanapadas** (listed in Buddhist texts such as the Anguttara Nikaya) by the 6th century BCE; **Magadha** rose (fertile land, iron ores, rivers, able rulers; capitals Rajagriha then Pataliputra)

steps.title: Buddhism and Jainism
steps.body:
- **Gautama Buddha** (6th–5th century BCE): born Lumbini; enlightenment Bodh Gaya; first sermon Sarnath; passed away at Kushinagar. **Four Noble Truths**, **Eightfold Path**, Middle Way
- **Vardhamana Mahavira**: 24th tirthankara; five vows — ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya; three jewels (right faith, knowledge, conduct)
- Both rejected animal sacrifice and the exclusivity of Brahmanical ritual and preached in Prakrit/Pali

steps.title: Solved: why Magadha?
steps.body:
- Fertile middle Ganga plains → surplus
- Iron deposits nearby → tools and weapons
- Rivers for transport and defence
- Ambitious rulers (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru; later Nandas, then Mauryas)

steps.title: Solved: compare the faiths
steps.body: Both: non-violence, karma, monastic orders. Differences: Buddhism's Middle Way vs Jainism's stricter asceticism; Buddhism spread widely outside India while Jainism remained concentrated in India (especially Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the first sermon at Bodh Gaya (it was Sarnath).
- Calling Mahavira the founder of Jainism (he was the 24th tirthankara).
- Giving exact dates for the Buddha's life as settled facts.
- Assuming Vedic and Harappan cultures were the same.

activity.prompt: Match the place to the event in the Buddha's life.

quiz.why: In Jain tradition, Mahavira was the 24th and last tirthankara.
The Rig Veda is the earliest and oldest Vedic text.

quiz.q: Number of Mahajanapadas in Buddhist texts:
quiz.why: Buddhist texts such as the Anguttara Nikaya list 16 Mahajanapadas.

quiz.q: Not one of Mahavira's five vows:
quiz.why: Mahavira's five vows include ahimsa, satya, asteya, brahmacharya and aparigraha. 'Satyagraha' is a Gandhian term.

quiz.q: A key reason for Magadha's rise:
quiz.why: Magadha rose because of iron ore deposits and fertile land, which helped agriculture, tools and weapons.

scenes.text: After the bloody Kalinga war, Ashoka inscribed his remorse on a rock edict.
His edicts, read again in 1837 when James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi, are among India's earliest royal messages.

steps.title: Mauryas (c. 321–185 BCE)
steps.body:
- **Chandragupta Maurya** with **Kautilya** (Arthashastra on statecraft); Greek envoy **Megasthenes** (Indica, surviving in fragments)
- **Ashoka**: Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE) described in **Rock Edict XIII**; **dhamma** — tolerance, non-violence, respect for elders, welfare; dhamma-mahamattas
- Edicts mostly in **Prakrit** using **Brahmi** script (Kharosthi in the north-west; Greek and Aramaic in Afghanistan)
- Third Buddhist council at Pataliputra (tradition)

steps.title: Guptas (c. 320–550 CE)
steps.body:
- **Chandragupta I** begins the Gupta era (c. 319–320 CE)
- **Samudragupta**: conquests recorded in the **Prayag (Allahabad) pillar inscription** composed by **Harishena**
- **Chandragupta II**: patron of arts; Chinese pilgrim **Faxian (Fa-Hien)** visited
- Achievements: **Aryabhata** (*Aryabhatiya*, 499 CE), Kalidasa's works, Nalanda's beginnings, temple architecture
- 'Golden Age' label is debated — prosperity for elites, but also land grants, feudal tendencies and caste rigidity

steps.title: Solved: source criticism
steps.body:
The Prayag inscription praises Samudragupta as unconquerable.

- It is a **prashasti** (court eulogy) — valuable for names and campaigns, but one-sided
- Cross-check with coins, other inscriptions and foreign accounts

steps.title: Solved: interpreting dhamma
steps.body: Ashoka's dhamma was not a call to convert everyone to Buddhism; it promoted ethical conduct and tolerance across sects — arguably also a tool for holding together a vast, diverse empire.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Ashoka's edicts are in Sanskrit.
- Treating Megasthenes' Indica as complete (only fragments survive in later writers).
- Calling the Gupta period 'golden' for everyone without qualification.
- Confusing Chandragupta Maurya with Chandragupta I or II.

activity.prompt: Order these events.

lessons.title: Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara and the Mughals

scenes.text: Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued bronze/copper token coins to stand in for silver.
Forgers flooded the market, and the experiment had to be withdrawn — an early lesson in monetary trust.

steps.title: Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)
steps.body:
- **Qutbuddin Aibak** (1206); **Iltutmish** consolidated rule, issued the silver **tanka** and copper **jital**; **iqta** system of revenue assignments
- **Alauddin Khalji** (1296–1316): market regulation and price control, defence against Mongols
- **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** (1325–51): shift of capital to Daulatabad, token currency
- Lodis ended at the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)**

steps.title: Vijayanagara and the Mughals
steps.body:
- **Vijayanagara** founded 1336 by Harihara and Bukka; peak under **Krishnadeva Raya**; defeated at **Talikota (1565)**; ruins at Hampi
- **Babur** defeats Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat (1526)
- **Akbar** (r. 1556–1605): Second Battle of Panipat (1556); **mansabdari** (rank-based nobility), **zabt** land revenue system associated with Raja Todar Mal, **sulh-i-kul** (universal peace), discussions at the Ibadat Khana (Fatehpur Sikri)
- **Bhakti**: Kabir, Guru Nanak, Mirabai, Tulsidas — devotion beyond ritual and caste; **Sufi**: Chishti order — Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi)

steps.title: Solved: institution and purpose
steps.body:
- **Iqta**: assigning revenue of territories to officers in return for military service → central control over nobles
- **Mansabdari**: ranks (zat and sawar) fixing pay and cavalry obligations → a graded, transferable nobility
- **Zabt**: measurement-based revenue assessment → predictable state income

steps.title: Solved: why did Tughlaq's token currency fail?
steps.body:
- Coins were easy to forge and the state could not control issue
- People hoarded silver and paid taxes in tokens
- Lesson: fiat money needs trust and anti-counterfeiting capacity

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the First (1526) and Second (1556) Battles of Panipat.
- Calling sulh-i-kul a new religion.
- Placing Vijayanagara's founding under the Mughals.
- Treating Bhakti and Sufi movements as opposed (they shared ideas of devotion and equality).

story.title: A battle in a mango grove

scenes.text: At Plassey in 1757, Robert Clive's small force won largely because the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar defected.
Within eight years the Company held the diwani — the right to collect revenue — of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

steps.title: Expansion
steps.body:
- **Plassey (1757)**: Clive defeats Siraj-ud-Daulah
- **Buxar (1764)**: Company defeats the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II
- **Diwani (1765)** by the Treaty of Allahabad
- **Regulating Act (1773)**; Pitt's India Act (1784)
- **Subsidiary alliance** (Wellesley, from 1798); **doctrine of lapse** (Dalhousie; e.g. Satara 1848, Jhansi and Nagpur 1854)
- Social reform: **sati abolished (1829)** under Bentinck, with Raja Ram Mohan Roy's campaign; **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856)** with Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar

steps.title: Land revenue systems
steps.body:
- **Permanent Settlement (1793)**, Cornwallis, mainly Bengal: zamindars pay a fixed revenue in perpetuity
- **Ryotwari**, associated with Thomas Munro, Madras and Bombay: direct settlement with cultivators (ryots), periodically revised
- **Mahalwari** (from 1822, Holt Mackenzie; North-Western Provinces, Punjab): settlement with village communities (mahals)
- Common effects: high demands, rigid collection, rise of moneylenders, land alienation

steps.title: Solved: compare the settlements
steps.body:
- Who paid the state? Zamindar (Permanent) / ryot (Ryotwari) / village body (Mahalwari)
- Was revenue fixed forever? Only under the Permanent Settlement
- Main winner: zamindars under the Permanent Settlement; the state under periodically revised systems

steps.title: Solved: doctrine of lapse
steps.body: A ruler of a dependent state died without a natural heir. Under Dalhousie's policy the state 'lapsed' to the Company — adopted sons were not recognised as heirs for succession. Jhansi's annexation became a grievance behind 1857.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating diwani to 1757.
- Associating Ryotwari with Bengal.
- Mixing up Wellesley (subsidiary alliance) and Dalhousie (lapse).
- Treating Company rule as purely 'trade' — it became a territorial power.

activity.prompt: Match the policy to the person.

quiz.why: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757, when Robert Clive defeated the Nawab of Bengal.
The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis.
Mahalwari settled land revenue with village communities. 'Mahal' means estate or village.
The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act was passed in 1856, after Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar's campaign.

quiz.q: Diwani was granted by the Treaty of:
quiz.why: The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, from Shah Alam II.

scenes.text: Sepoys at Meerut, punished for refusing new cartridges, broke out and marched to Delhi.
They proclaimed the aged Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader. Revolt spread across north and central India.

steps.title: Causes and course
steps.body:
- **Political**: annexations (doctrine of lapse, Awadh 1856)
- **Economic**: heavy land revenue, ruin of artisans
- **Socio-religious**: fear of interference with customs
- **Military**: grievances of sepoys; the immediate trigger was the **Enfield rifle cartridges** rumoured to be greased with animal fat
- Centres and leaders: Delhi (Bahadur Shah Zafar, Bakht Khan), Kanpur (Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Bihar (Kunwar Singh)
- Suppressed by 1858–59 with great loss of life on all sides

steps.title: Consequences and interpretations
steps.body:
- **Government of India Act, 1858**: Crown takes over from the Company; Secretary of State for India; Governor-General also Viceroy
- Queen's Proclamation (1858): non-interference in religion, end of annexation policy
- Army reorganised; 'divide and rule' strategies grew
- Interpretations: 'sepoy mutiny' (colonial view), 'first war of independence' (V. D. Savarkar, 1909), a broad popular uprising with varied local causes (many modern historians)

steps.title: Solved: why did it fail?
steps.body:
- Limited geographical spread (south and east largely unaffected)
- Lack of a unified leadership and programme
- Many princes and elites sided with the British
- Superior British resources, telegraph and railways

steps.title: Solved: source question
steps.body: Two accounts: a British officer's diary calls the rebels 'mutineers'; a proclamation from Delhi calls on Hindus and Muslims to unite against foreign rule. Use both: each reveals its author's position — compare, don't simply believe either.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling it a purely military mutiny.
- Saying 1857 led to immediate independence.
- Ignoring the role of peasants and artisans.
- Dating the Government of India Act to 1857.

quiz.q: A reason for the revolt's failure:
options: it was in the south only
quiz.why: The revolt failed partly for lack of unified leadership and coordination. The rebels were scattered, and the British had superior resources.

lessons.title: The national movement: 1885 to Quit India

scenes.text: On 12 March 1930, Gandhi set out from Sabarmati with 78 followers; on 6 April he picked up salt at Dandi.
A simple act against an unjust tax drew millions into civil disobedience.

steps.title: Phases
steps.body:
- **Indian National Congress** founded 1885 in Bombay (first president W. C. Bonnerjee; A. O. Hume a founder member); **moderates** (Naoroji's drain theory, petitions)
- **Partition of Bengal (1905)** by Curzon → **Swadeshi and boycott**; Surat split (1907); Morley–Minto reforms (1909) with separate electorates; partition annulled 1911
- **Lucknow Pact (1916)** between Congress and the Muslim League; Home Rule Leagues (Tilak, Annie Besant)
- Gandhi's early campaigns: **Champaran (1917)**, Kheda and Ahmedabad (1918)
- **Rowlatt Act** protests; **Jallianwala Bagh massacre, 13 April 1919**
- **Non-Cooperation (1920–22)**, withdrawn after **Chauri Chaura (February 1922)**
- Simon Commission boycott (1928); **Lahore session (1929)**: Purna Swaraj; **Civil Disobedience** with the **Dandi March (1930)**; Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931); Poona Pact (1932); Government of India Act 1935
- **Quit India**, launched **8 August 1942** ('Do or Die'); INA under Subhas Chandra Bose

steps.title: Solved: methods compared
steps.body:
- Moderates: petitions, memoranda, economic critique (drain of wealth)
- Extremists/Swadeshi: boycott of foreign goods, national education
- Gandhian: mass non-violent satyagraha — non-cooperation, civil disobedience, constructive programme (khadi, Hindu–Muslim unity, removal of untouchability)

steps.title: Solved: why salt?
steps.body: Salt was used by everyone, rich or poor, and the tax was visibly unjust; breaking the law was easy and non-violent; it connected an everyday grievance to the demand for swaraj.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating Jallianwala Bagh to 1920.
- Mixing up Non-Cooperation (1920) and Civil Disobedience (1930).
- Saying the Congress demanded full independence in 1885 (that came in 1929).
- Ignoring revolutionaries, peasants, workers and women's roles.

activity.prompt: Order these events of the national movement.

quiz.why: W. C. Bonnerjee was the first president of the Indian National Congress, at Bombay in 1885.

quiz.q: Purna Swaraj resolution was passed at:
quiz.why: The Purna Swaraj (complete independence) resolution was passed at the Lahore session of 1929, under Nehru's presidency.

scenes.text: At midnight Nehru spoke of a 'tryst with destiny' as India became independent.
The same months saw partition — mass migration and terrible communal violence that displaced millions. Remembering both is part of honest history.

steps.title: The road to 1947
steps.body:
- **Cripps Mission (1942)** — offer of post-war dominion status, rejected
- **Cabinet Mission (1946)** — proposed a loose federation; elections to a Constituent Assembly
- Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) and communal violence
- **Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947)** → **Indian Independence Act (July 1947)** → independence on **15 August 1947**; boundaries drawn by the Radcliffe commission
- Partition caused one of the largest migrations in history; estimates of deaths vary widely (often cited from several hundred thousand to about a million or more)

steps.title: Integrating princely states
steps.body:
About 560 princely states were integrated, led by **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** with **V. P. Menon**, mainly through the **Instrument of Accession** and later merger agreements.

- **Junagadh**: plebiscite (1948) favoured India
- **Hyderabad**: police action, **Operation Polo (September 1948)**
- **Jammu and Kashmir**: Instrument of Accession signed in October 1947

steps.title: Solved: why partition?
steps.body: Historians stress several interacting factors: growth of communal politics and separate electorates; the Muslim League's demand for Pakistan (Lahore Resolution, 1940); failure of Congress–League negotiations; British haste to withdraw after the war; and escalating violence in 1946–47. Avoid single-cause answers.

steps.title: Solved: method of integration
steps.body: Instrument of Accession: rulers ceded defence, external affairs and communications to India. Later, merger agreements and constitutional changes brought states fully into the Union.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all princely states joined voluntarily on 15 August 1947.
- Giving a single precise death toll for partition as certain.
- Confusing the Cripps (1942) and Cabinet (1946) Missions.
- Treating partition as only a political event and ignoring its human cost.

- **Use**: what can it reliably tell us?
