courses.title: Sociology I · concepts and classical thinkers
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Basic sociological concepts, socialisation and research methods, and the classical thinkers Durkheim, Marx and Weber with their key works and ideas.
outcomes: Learners can define culture, norms, status, role and socialisation and choose research methods
Learners can explain Durkheim's social facts, solidarity and suicide types
Learners can explain Marx's materialism, class and alienation
Learners can explain Weber's social action, ideal types, authority and the Protestant ethic

story.title: One job loss, a million job losses

scenes.text: When one person loses a job, it's a personal trouble. When millions do in a recession, it's a public issue.
C. Wright Mills called the ability to link the two 'the sociological imagination' (1959).

steps.title: Core concepts
steps.body:
- **Auguste Comte** coined 'sociology'; positivism; law of three stages (theological, metaphysical, positive)
- **Society**, **culture** (material and non-material), **norms** (folkways, mores, laws), **values**
- **Status** (ascribed vs achieved) and **role** (role conflict, role strain)
- **Socialisation**: primary (family) and secondary (school, peers, media, workplace); resocialisation
- **Groups**: primary (Cooley) vs secondary; reference groups

steps.title: Research methods
steps.body:
- Quantitative: surveys, questionnaires, statistical analysis
- Qualitative: participant observation, interviews, case studies, ethnography
- Sampling: random, stratified, purposive, snowball
- Ethics: informed consent, anonymity, avoiding harm
- Reflexivity: the researcher's position shapes findings

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body:
- Being born into a family → **ascribed** status; becoming a doctor → **achieved** status
- A working mother torn between office and child's school event → **role conflict**
- Learning table manners at home → **primary socialisation**

steps.title: Solved: choose a method
steps.body:
Topic: everyday life of street vendors.

- Best: **participant observation and interviews** (rich, contextual data)
- If the question is 'what % of vendors use UPI?', a **survey** with a representative sample is better

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating personal troubles and public issues as unrelated.
- Confusing norms (rules) with values (ideals).
- Assuming qualitative research is 'unscientific'.
- Forgetting ethics in studies of vulnerable groups.

activity.prompt: Ascribed or achieved status?

quiz.why: Auguste Comte coined the word 'sociology', and he founded positivism.
The Sociological Imagination (1959) is by C. Wright Mills. It links personal troubles to public issues.

quiz.q: Family is the main agent of:
quiz.why: The family is the main agent of primary socialisation, in a person's early years.
Mores are norms with strong moral weight, whose violation is seriously condemned. Folkways are casual customs.

quiz.q: Best method for studying lived experience in depth:
quiz.why: Participant observation gives in-depth, qualitative understanding of lived experience.

scenes.text: Durkheim noticed that suicide rates differed steadily between groups and countries year after year.
He argued social integration and regulation — not just individual psychology — shape such rates.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Social facts**: ways of acting, thinking and feeling external to individuals and exercising constraint (*The Rules of Sociological Method*, 1895)
- **The Division of Labour in Society** (1893): **mechanical solidarity** (similarity; repressive law; simple societies) vs **organic solidarity** (interdependence through specialisation; restitutive law)
- **Suicide** (1897): **egoistic** (low integration), **altruistic** (excessive integration), **anomic** (low regulation, e.g. sudden economic change), **fatalistic** (excessive regulation)
- **The Elementary Forms of Religious Life** (1912): sacred vs profane; religion as collective representation
- **Anomie**: normlessness during rapid change

steps.title: Solved: classify the suicide type
steps.body:
- An isolated elderly person with no social ties → **egoistic**
- A sudden market crash leaves people without stable norms → **anomic**
- A soldier sacrificing life for the group → **altruistic**
- A person under oppressively strict control → **fatalistic**

(Sociological categories only; any real person at risk needs help — Tele-MANAS 14416.)

steps.title: Solved: solidarity
steps.body: A village where everyone farms and shares rituals → **mechanical**. A metro city where people depend on doctors, drivers, coders and farmers they never meet → **organic**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping mechanical and organic solidarity.
- Thinking Durkheim explained suicide by individual psychology.
- Confusing anomie (normlessness) with alienation (Marx).
- Using his typology to label real individuals rather than social patterns.

activity.prompt: Match Durkheim's concept to its meaning.
pairs: External, constraining way of acting or thinking

quiz.q: The Division of Labour in Society:
quiz.why: Durkheim's The Division of Labour in Society was published in 1893.
Organic solidarity is based on interdependence, as people specialise and depend on each other. Mechanical solidarity is based on similarity.

quiz.q: Suicide linked to sudden economic disruption:
quiz.why: Anomic suicide is linked to sudden disruption, like an economic crash, which weakens social regulation.
Durkheim's Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912) discusses the distinction between the sacred and the profane.
Durkheim's social facts are external to the individual and constraining on them.

scenes.text: An assembly-line worker fits one part into thousands of phones a day but could never afford one.
Marx would call this alienation — and ask who owns the factory and gets the surplus.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Historical materialism**: the economic **base** (forces and relations of production) shapes the **superstructure** (law, politics, religion, ideology)
- **Class struggle**: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' (*The Communist Manifesto*, 1848, with Engels)
- **Bourgeoisie** (owners of means of production) vs **proletariat** (sell labour power)
- **Surplus value**: value produced by workers beyond their wages (*Capital*, Vol. I, 1867)
- **Alienation** from the product, the process, one's species-being and other people
- **Class in itself** vs **class for itself** (class consciousness); false consciousness

steps.title: Solved: surplus value
steps.body:
A worker paid ₹600 a day produces goods worth ₹1,500 (after materials).

- Surplus value = ₹1,500 − ₹600 = **₹900** appropriated by the owner (Marx's framework)

steps.title: Solved: base and superstructure
steps.body: Laws protecting private property and contracts are part of the superstructure that, in Marx's view, stabilise capitalist relations of production in the base.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating Marx's sociology with any particular later government.
- Confusing alienation with anomie.
- Thinking base–superstructure is a one-way, mechanical relation in all readings (many Marxists stress interaction).
- Calling all wage earners 'bourgeoisie'.

items.back: Workers don't own or control what they make
Work is repetitive and directed by others
Work no longer expresses human creativity

quiz.q: The Communist Manifesto was published in:
quiz.why: The Communist Manifesto was published in 1848, by Marx and Engels.

quiz.q: Owners of the means of production:
quiz.why: In Marx, the bourgeoisie are the owners of the means of production. The proletariat sell their labour.
Surplus value is the value workers create beyond their wages, which the owners keep. Marx saw it as the source of exploitation.

quiz.q: Law and religion belong to the:
quiz.why: Law and religion belong to the superstructure, shaped by the economic base, in Marx's theory.

quiz.q: Class becoming aware of its interests:
quiz.why: A class that is aware of its common interests and acts on them is a 'class for itself'.

story.title: Why the office runs on files

scenes.text: A government office runs by written rules, fixed hierarchy and files — regardless of who sits in which chair.
Weber saw bureaucracy as the most efficient form of legal-rational organisation — and feared its 'iron cage'.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Verstehen**: interpretive understanding of the meanings actors give to action
- **Types of social action**: instrumentally rational, value-rational, affectual, traditional
- **Ideal type**: an analytical model built by accentuating features (not a moral ideal)
- ***The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism*** (1904–05): Calvinist ideas of calling and worldly asceticism had an elective affinity with the capitalist spirit
- **Authority**: traditional, charismatic, legal-rational
- **Bureaucracy**: hierarchy, written rules, specialisation, impersonality, merit-based appointment; the **iron cage** of rationalisation
- Stratification: **class, status and party**

steps.title: Solved: classify the action
steps.body:
- Choosing the cheapest flight to reach a meeting → **instrumentally rational**
- Refusing a bribe because it is wrong, whatever the cost → **value-rational**
- Hugging a friend who passed an exam → **affectual**
- Touching elders' feet because it has always been done → **traditional**

steps.title: Solved: Weber vs Marx
steps.body: Marx: economic base drives ideas. Weber: ideas (e.g. religious ethics) can also shape economic life, and stratification has several dimensions (class, status, party), not class alone.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating an 'ideal type' as the best or perfect form.
- Saying Weber argued Protestantism alone caused capitalism (he argued an affinity among several factors).
- Mixing his three types of authority with his four types of action.

activity.prompt: Which type of social action (Weber)?

items.text: Comparing prices online to buy a laptop
Donating anonymously out of religious duty
Celebrating a festival as the family always has
Choosing a course for its job prospects

quiz.why: Verstehen is Weber's term for interpretive understanding: grasping the meanings people attach to their actions.

quiz.q: The Protestant Ethic was published in:
quiz.why: Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism appeared as two essays in 1904–05.
Weber's 'iron cage' refers to rationalised, bureaucratic life that traps people in rules and efficiency.
Weber's three dimensions of stratification are class, status and party.
An ideal type is an analytical model that stresses key features for comparison. It is not a moral ideal or an average.

questions.q: Sociology studies:
questions.why: Sociology studies society and social relationships.

questions.q: Suicide (1897) was written by:
questions.why: Suicide (1897) was written by Émile Durkheim.

questions.q: Capital, Vol. I (1867):
questions.why: Capital, Volume I (1867), is by Karl Marx.

questions.q: Achieved status example:
questions.why: An achieved status is earned by effort, like being a doctor. Sex, age and caste at birth are ascribed.

questions.q: Unity through specialisation:
questions.why: Unity through specialisation and interdependence is organic solidarity, in Durkheim.

questions.q: Bureaucracy is associated with:
questions.why: Bureaucracy is associated with Weber's legal-rational authority.

questions.q: Assertion: Durkheim treated suicide rates as social facts. Reason: Rates varied systematically with integration and regulation across groups.
questions.why: Durkheim treated suicide rates as social facts because they varied systematically with social integration and regulation. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Worker paid ₹500 produces value ₹1,200 (net of materials). Surplus value:
questions.why: Surplus value = value produced − wages = 1,200 − 500 = ₹700.

questions.q: Value-rational action example:
options: telling the truth despite personal loss
questions.why: Value-rational action is done for a belief in a value, whatever the cost. Telling the truth despite personal loss is an example.

questions.q: Case: After sudden demonetisation-type shocks, a study finds a spike in confusion and normlessness among small traders. Durkheim's concept:
questions.why: A spike in confusion and normlessness after a sudden shock is anomie, in Durkheim's sense: a breakdown of social regulation.

questions.q: Weber's argument in the Protestant Ethic is best described as:
options: Protestantism was the sole cause of capitalism
religious ideas had an elective affinity with the capitalist spirit
questions.why: Weber argued that Protestant religious ideas had an elective affinity with the capitalist spirit. He did not say it was the sole cause.

questions.q: Marx's false consciousness means:
options: workers adopting ideas that serve the ruling class
questions.why: False consciousness, in Marx, means workers adopting ideas that serve the ruling class's interests, against their own.

questions.q: Which pairing is INCORRECT?
questions.why: Mechanical solidarity belongs to Durkheim, not Weber. The other pairings are correct.

questions.q: A researcher joins a village festival committee for a year to study rituals. Method and a key risk:
questions.why: Joining a village festival committee for a year is participant observation. A key risk is researcher bias, or 'going native'.

questions.q: Altruistic suicide in Durkheim's scheme is linked to:
questions.why: In Durkheim's typology, altruistic suicide is linked to excessive social integration, where the individual is subordinated to the group.

courses.title: Sociology II · Indian society: caste, kinship, tribe, change
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Caste and its transformations, family, kinship and marriage in India, tribal communities and constitutional safeguards, and social change through modernisation, urbanisation and social movements — discussed respectfully and factually.
outcomes: Learners can explain caste features, sanskritisation and dominant caste
Learners can compare family types, descent systems and marriage rules
Learners can describe Scheduled Tribes and protective provisions
Learners can analyse processes of change and key social movements

scenes.text: In a village, a family from a historically marginalised caste opens the first computer centre; youth of all castes now train there.
Caste persists in many ways, yet education, law and markets are changing its shape. Sociologists study both continuity and change.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Varna** (fourfold scriptural scheme) vs **jati** (thousands of local endogamous groups that operate in practice)
- **G. S. Ghurye's features**: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on commensality and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities, restricted choice of occupation, **endogamy**
- **Louis Dumont** (*Homo Hierarchicus*, 1966): purity and pollution as the organising principle
- **M. N. Srinivas**: **sanskritisation** (lower castes adopting customs of higher castes to claim status), **westernisation**, and **dominant caste** (numerical strength, land, political power) — from his Coorg and Rampura studies
- Constitution: Art 15 (no discrimination), **Art 17 (untouchability abolished)**, reservations for SCs/STs/OBCs; laws such as the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

steps.title: Solved: name the process
steps.body:
- A caste group gives up meat-eating and adopts Sanskritic rituals to claim higher status → **sanskritisation**
- A family adopts English education, Western dress and lifestyles → **westernisation**
- A landowning, numerous caste dominates village politics → **dominant caste**

steps.title: Solved: continuity and change
steps.body:
Change: urban jobs, education, inter-caste marriages (still a minority), political mobilisation of marginalised groups.
Continuity: endogamy remains common; discrimination persists in places — documented by studies and court cases. Balanced answers cite both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating varna and jati as the same thing.
- Claiming caste has disappeared in cities.
- Using caste slurs or stereotypes in answers — use respectful, constitutional terms.
- Confusing sanskritisation with westernisation.

activity.prompt: Match the concept to the scholar.

quiz.why: Article 17 of the Constitution abolishes untouchability.
M. N. Srinivas coined 'Sanskritisation', in his study of the Coorgs.
Endogamy means marrying within one's own group, such as caste.
In Srinivas's concept, a dominant caste has large numbers, land ownership and political power in a village.
Homo Hierarchicus (1966) is by Louis Dumont.

scenes.text: Nani grew up in a joint family of 25 people under one roof and one kitchen.
Her grandchildren live in nuclear families in different cities — yet still gather for every festival. Families change form, but kinship ties remain.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Joint family**: several generations sharing residence, property and kitchen; **nuclear family**: couple and unmarried children
- Many urban families are 'functionally joint' — separate homes but shared obligations
- **Descent**: patrilineal (most of India), **matrilineal** (Khasi and Garo of Meghalaya; historically the Nairs of Kerala), bilateral
- **Residence**: patrilocal, matrilocal, neolocal
- **Marriage rules**: endogamy (within caste/community), exogamy (outside clan/gotra); cross-cousin marriage more common in South Indian kinship patterns
- **Iravati Karve** (*Kinship Organisation in India*, 1953) mapped regional kinship zones
- Legal changes: Hindu Marriage Act 1955; Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 gave daughters equal coparcenary rights; Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body:
- Property and family name pass through the mother's line → **matrilineal** (e.g. Khasi)
- A newly married couple sets up home in a new city → **neolocal**
- Marriage forbidden within the same gotra → **gotra exogamy**

steps.title: Solved: is the joint family disappearing?
steps.body: Evidence of change: urbanisation and migration increase nuclear households. Evidence of continuity: strong support networks, elder care, shared financial decisions. Sociologists like A. M. Shah argued household form changes cyclically and the joint family ideal persists.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating matrilineal with matriarchal (descent through women does not mean women hold all power).
- Assuming all rural families are joint and all urban ones nuclear.
- Confusing endogamy with exogamy.

activity.prompt: Endogamy or exogamy?

items.text: Village exogamy in parts of North India

quiz.why: The Khasi of Meghalaya are matrilineal: descent is traced through the mother.
Kinship Organisation in India (1953) is by Iravati Karve, who described regional kinship zones.

quiz.q: Couple living in a new independent home:
quiz.why: A couple living in a new, independent home is neolocal residence.

quiz.q: Daughters got equal coparcenary rights by:
quiz.why: The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, gave daughters equal coparcenary rights.
Matrilineal means descent is traced through the mother's line. It doesn't mean women rule.

scenes.text: A forest-dwelling community has gathered mahua and tendu leaves for generations, but has no paper title to the land.
The Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognised such rights — showing how law and community life intersect.

steps.title: Key facts
steps.body:
- **Scheduled Tribes** notified under Article 342; about 8.6% of India's population (Census 2011)
- **Fifth Schedule**: Scheduled Areas and Tribes Advisory Councils in several states
- **Sixth Schedule**: Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
- **PESA Act, 1996**: extends panchayati raj to Fifth Schedule areas, empowering gram sabhas
- **Forest Rights Act, 2006**: recognises individual and community forest rights
- Debates: isolation vs assimilation vs integration (Verrier Elwin, G. S. Ghurye, Nehru's 'Panchsheel' for tribal policy); displacement by dams and mines; identity and indigeneity

steps.title: Solved: which provision?
steps.body:
- A gram sabha in a Scheduled Area must be consulted before land acquisition → **PESA 1996**
- A Khasi district council makes rules on land and customs → **Sixth Schedule**
- A community claims rights to collect forest produce → **Forest Rights Act 2006**

steps.title: Solved: debates
steps.body: Elwin initially favoured protecting tribal ways of life; Ghurye saw tribes as 'backward Hindus' to be assimilated; Nehru's policy sought integration while respecting tribal culture and rights. Modern views emphasise self-determination and consent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating all tribal communities as identical.
- Confusing Fifth and Sixth Schedules.
- Using outdated or derogatory terms ('primitive') — use 'Scheduled Tribes' or the community's own name; 'Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups' is the official term for the most vulnerable.

activity.prompt: Match the provision to its purpose.
pairs: Autonomous District Councils in the North-East
Gram sabha powers in Scheduled Areas

quiz.q: Autonomous District Councils are under the:
quiz.why: Autonomous District Councils in the North-East come under the Sixth Schedule.
The PESA Act (Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas) was passed in 1996.
Scheduled Tribes were about 8.6% of India's population in the 2011 Census.
The Forest Rights Act, 2006, recognises individual and community rights of forest dwellers.
Scheduled Tribes are notified under Article 342. Article 341 is for Scheduled Castes.

scenes.text: In 1973 in Chamoli, women and villagers embraced trees to stop commercial felling.
The Chipko movement became a symbol of ecological and women's activism worldwide.

steps.title: Processes
steps.body:
- **Modernisation**: industrialisation, secularisation, rational-legal institutions (Yogendra Singh's *Modernization of Indian Tradition*, 1973)
- **Westernisation** and **sanskritisation** (Srinivas)
- **Urbanisation**: urban share about 31% in Census 2011; migration, slums, new middle classes
- **Globalisation**: IT and service jobs, consumer culture, cultural hybridity, new inequalities
- **Gender**: education and work participation changes; laws on dowry, domestic violence (2005), workplace harassment (POSH Act 2013)

steps.title: Social movements
steps.body:
- Characteristics: collective action, shared identity, sustained over time, aims at change
- Types: reformist, revolutionary, redemptive, alternative; 'old' (class-based) vs 'new' social movements (environment, gender, identity)
- Examples: **Chipko (1973)** — Gaura Devi, Chandi Prasad Bhatt, Sunderlal Bahuguna; **Narmada Bachao Andolan** (from the mid-1980s; Medha Patkar); Dalit movements inspired by Ambedkar; women's movements; farmers' movements

steps.title: Solved: classify the movement
steps.body:
- Chipko → **new social movement** (ecology, livelihood, women's participation); reformist in aims
- A movement seeking complete overthrow of an economic system → **revolutionary**

steps.title: Solved: urbanisation effects
steps.body: Push factors (rural distress) and pull factors (jobs) drive migration; outcomes include informal work, slums, and weaker caste controls in public spaces — but also new forms of exclusion (e.g. housing discrimination).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating modernisation as identical to westernisation.
- Assuming social movements always succeed or always fail.
- Giving precise statistics you are not sure of — state the source and year if you quote numbers.

activity.prompt: Order these social milestones.

events.text: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act
POSH Act on workplace sexual harassment

quiz.why: The Chipko movement began in 1973, in Chamoli (now in Uttarakhand).

quiz.q: Narmada Bachao Andolan is linked to:
quiz.why: The Narmada Bachao Andolan is linked with Medha Patkar, against big dams on the Narmada.

quiz.q: Urban share of India's population (Census 2011) about:
quiz.why: In the 2011 Census, about 31% of India's population was urban (31.1%).
Modernization of Indian Tradition (1973) is by Yogendra Singh.

quiz.q: A 'new social movement' typically focuses on:
quiz.why: New social movements focus on identity, environment and gender, rather than only class and wages.

questions.q: Jati refers to:
questions.why: Jati refers to local, endogamous caste groups. It is the operational unit of caste, while varna is the four-fold division.

questions.q: A nuclear family consists of:
questions.why: A nuclear family consists of parents and their unmarried children.

questions.q: Chipko movement concerned:
questions.why: The Chipko movement concerned forests, and protecting trees from felling.

questions.q: Sixth Schedule applies to:
questions.why: The Sixth Schedule applies to tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.

questions.q: Westernisation is a concept of:
questions.why: Westernisation is a concept of M. N. Srinivas, in Social Change in Modern India.

questions.q: Gotra exogamy forbids marriage:
questions.why: Gotra exogamy forbids marriage within the same gotra (clan).

questions.q: Assertion: Matrilineal descent does not mean matriarchy. Reason: Authority in many matrilineal groups may rest with maternal uncles or men.
questions.why: Matrilineal descent is about tracing descent, not about power. In many matrilineal groups authority rests with maternal uncles or men. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which law empowers gram sabhas in Scheduled Areas?
questions.why: PESA (1996) empowers gram sabhas in Scheduled Areas.

questions.q: A group adopting vegetarianism and Sanskritic rituals to claim status:
questions.why: A group adopting vegetarianism and Sanskritic rituals to claim higher status is sanskritisation.

questions.q: Case: A study finds inter-caste marriages rising in cities but still a small share of all marriages. Best conclusion:
options: caste endogamy is weakening slowly but persists
questions.why: Rising but still small inter-caste marriages in cities suggest caste endogamy is weakening slowly but persists.

questions.q: Dumont saw the caste system as organised by:
questions.why: Dumont saw caste as organised by the ideology of purity and pollution, in Homo Hierarchicus.

questions.q: Which is a reason the joint-family ideal persists in cities?
options: functional ties of support and shared obligations
questions.why: The joint-family ideal persists in cities through functional ties of mutual support and shared obligations, even when households are separate.

questions.q: Which statement about tribal policy debates is accurate?
options: positions ranged from protection (early Elwin) to assimilation (Ghurye) to integration (Nehru)
the Sixth Schedule covers all states
questions.why: Debates on tribal policy ranged from protection (early Elwin) to assimilation (Ghurye) to integration (Nehru). So it is wrong that everyone agreed on assimilation.

questions.q: Daughters' coparcenary rights in Hindu joint family property were equalised by:
options: the 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act
questions.why: Daughters' coparcenary rights in Hindu joint family property were equalised by the 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act.

questions.q: Chipko is best classified as:
options: a new social movement blending ecology, livelihood and gender
questions.why: Chipko is a new social movement that blends ecology, livelihood and gender concerns, since village women played a major role.

courses.title: BA Sociology · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: Thinker and concept sheets for Sociology, a solved case-question set and a 15-question mock exam.
outcomes: Learners can recall thinkers, books and concepts
Learners can apply concepts to Indian examples
Learners can write balanced analytical answers

scenes.text: Durkheim, Marx, Weber — three lenses on the same society.
Try explaining one event (say, a factory strike) through each lens.

steps.title: Thinkers
steps.body:
- Comte: coined sociology; positivism; three stages
- Durkheim: Division of Labour 1893; Rules 1895; Suicide 1897; Elementary Forms 1912; social facts, solidarity, anomie
- Marx: Manifesto 1848; Capital 1867; base–superstructure, class, surplus value, alienation
- Weber: Protestant Ethic 1904–05; verstehen, ideal type, social action, authority, bureaucracy, class–status–party
- Mills: Sociological Imagination 1959

steps.title: Indian sociology
steps.body:
- Ghurye: features of caste; Srinivas: sanskritisation, westernisation, dominant caste; Dumont: purity–pollution
- Karve: kinship zones (1953); Yogendra Singh: modernisation (1973)
- STs ≈ 8.6% (2011); Fifth/Sixth Schedules; PESA 1996; FRA 2006
- Chipko 1973; NBA mid-1980s

steps.title: Answer frame
steps.body: Define → explain with a thinker → apply to an Indian example → note a criticism → conclude.

cards.back: Separation of workers from product, process, species-being and others (Marx)
Numerical, economic and political dominance in a locality (Srinivas)
Couple sets up a new independent home

quiz.why: Elementary Forms of Religious Life is by Durkheim (1912).
Class, status and party are Weber's dimensions of stratification.
The purity–pollution model of caste is Louis Dumont's.
Article 341 is for notifying Scheduled Castes. Article 342 is for Scheduled Tribes.
Auguste Comte proposed the law of three stages: theological, metaphysical and positive.

scenes.text: Workers at a garment factory go on strike over wages and safety.
Each founding thinker would highlight something different.

steps.title: Marx's lens
steps.body: Conflict between owners and workers over surplus value; strike as a step from class in itself to class for itself.

steps.title: Durkheim's lens
steps.body: Rapid industrial change without adequate regulation produces anomie; restitutive law and occupational associations could restore solidarity.

steps.title: Weber's lens
steps.body: Workers' meanings and motives (verstehen); union bureaucracy as legal-rational organisation; status and party dimensions (e.g. caste or political affiliations shaping the strike).

activity.prompt: Match the observation to the thinker most likely to stress it.
pairs: Linking personal troubles to public issues

quiz.why: Restitutive law, aimed at repairing harm, goes with organic solidarity, in Durkheim. Repressive law goes with mechanical solidarity.
Union bureaucracy, with rules and offices, illustrates Weber's legal-rational organisation.
A strike as an expression of class consciousness is 'class for itself', in Marx.

quiz.q: Which lens focuses on meanings actors attach?
quiz.why: Weber's approach focuses on the meanings actors attach to their actions (verstehen).

quiz.q: Occupational associations to reduce anomie were proposed by:
quiz.why: Durkheim proposed occupational associations to reduce anomie, in the preface to The Division of Labour.

scenes.text: Twelve minutes for five short cases.
Name the concept, then explain in two lines.

steps.title: Model 1
steps.body: A migrant worker in a metro feels lonely and rootless → Durkheim's **anomie/low integration** and Mills's link to public issues of migration.

steps.title: Model 2
steps.body: A tribal gram sabha rejects a mining project after consultation → **PESA 1996** and **Forest Rights Act 2006** in action.

quiz.q: Gram sabha consent in Scheduled Areas:
quiz.why: PESA (1996) gives gram sabhas a say, including consent, in Scheduled Areas.
Feeling rootless amid rapid change is anomie, a state of normlessness in Durkheim's work.
Separate homes with shared obligations make a functionally joint family. It is not simply nuclear.

quiz.q: Ideal type is a tool of:
quiz.why: The ideal type is a methodological tool of Max Weber.

options: status mobility through adopting higher-caste customs
quiz.why: Sanskritisation, in Srinivas, is status mobility through adopting the customs of higher castes.

questions.q: Primary socialisation mainly occurs in the:
questions.why: Primary socialisation mainly occurs in the family, in early childhood.

questions.q: Bourgeoisie are:
questions.why: In Marx, the bourgeoisie are the owners of the means of production.

questions.q: Khasi society is:
questions.why: Khasi society, in Meghalaya, is matrilineal.

questions.q: Durkheim's study of suicide was published in:
questions.why: Durkheim's study of suicide was published in 1897.

questions.q: Article 17 relates to:
questions.why: Article 17 abolishes untouchability.

questions.q: Charismatic authority rests on:
questions.why: Charismatic authority rests on the exceptional personal qualities of a leader.

questions.q: Assertion: Weber's ideal type is not a moral ideal. Reason: It is an analytical construct exaggerating key features for comparison.
questions.why: Weber's ideal type is an analytical construct that exaggerates key features to allow comparison, not a moral ideal. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is an example of organic solidarity?
options: a city where people depend on many specialists
questions.why: A city where people depend on many specialists shows organic solidarity, based on interdependence. A monastery or hunting band shows mechanical solidarity.

questions.q: A couple living with the husband's parents:
questions.why: A couple living with the husband's parents is patrilocal residence.

questions.q: Case: After a factory closure, workers' families report rising alcoholism and broken routines. Best concept:
questions.why: After a factory closure, rising alcoholism and broken routines show a breakdown of regulation and normlessness: anomie.

questions.q: The Forest Rights Act (2006) is significant because it:
options: recognised historical injustice to forest dwellers
questions.why: The Forest Rights Act (2006) is significant because it recognised the historical injustice to forest dwellers by recognising their rights.

questions.q: A key difference between Marx and Weber on stratification:
options: Weber adds status and party to class
questions.why: Marx saw class as the main basis of stratification, while Weber adds status and party to class. So Weber's view is multidimensional.

questions.q: Which is the best example of 'personal troubles vs public issues'?
options: one graduate's unemployment vs mass graduate unemployment
questions.why: Mills's 'personal troubles vs public issues': one graduate's unemployment is a personal trouble, but mass graduate unemployment is a public issue.

questions.q: Which statement about the Indian joint family is most defensible?
options: household forms change, but joint-family obligations often continue
questions.why: Household forms change, but obligations of the joint family often continue. So it hasn't fully disappeared, and it isn't legally mandatory.

questions.q: Srinivas's dominant caste concept stresses:
options: local numerical, economic and political power
questions.why: Srinivas's dominant caste has local numerical strength, economic power (often land) and political power. It is not just ritual rank.
